INTERNET: PERSISTENT WORLD

ULTIMATE INTERNET SIMULATION — 2026 EDITION


THE VISION


Create an extraordinarily realistic, terminal-driven internet civilization simulator.


The player must feel as though they own and operate an actual computer connected to a living, evolving global internet.


The game must simulate the modern internet as a complex interconnected ecosystem of infrastructure, people, organizations, software, protocols, services, businesses, artificial intelligence, and digital communities.


This is a persistent sandbox with no mandatory storyline.


The player is not a superhero hacker. They are an ordinary individual entering a complex digital society.


Their identity, reputation, resources, skills, relationships, business interests, and technical infrastructure evolve naturally.


The game should prioritize simulation depth, technical authenticity, freedom, and emergent gameplay.


1. MODERN INTERNET ARCHITECTURE


Recreate the actual structure of the modern internet.


Include multiple interconnected layers:


PHYSICAL INFRASTRUCTURE:


- Fiber-optic networks.
- Submarine communication cables.
- Internet exchange points.
- Data centers.
- Telecommunications infrastructure.
- Cellular networks.
- Wi-Fi networks.
- Routers and switches.
- Residential internet connections.
- Satellite connectivity.


NETWORK INFRASTRUCTURE:


- IPv4 and IPv6.
- TCP and UDP.
- QUIC.
- HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.
- DNS and DNSSEC.
- DHCP.
- NAT.
- BGP and autonomous systems.
- RPKI.
- VPN infrastructure.
- Proxies.
- Reverse proxies.
- Network address management.
- Routing tables.
- Firewalls.


WEB INFRASTRUCTURE:


- HTML.
- CSS.
- JavaScript.
- Web APIs.
- REST APIs.
- GraphQL.
- WebSockets.
- WebTransport.
- WebRTC.
- TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3.
- Certificates and public key infrastructure.
- CDNs.
- Caching systems.


All technologies must have functional implementations within the simulated environment.


Different protocols should have distinct characteristics, compatibility requirements, security implications, and performance consequences.


2. COMPLETE OPERATING SYSTEM SIMULATION


The player's computer should function like a real Linux workstation.


Provide:


- Terminal emulator.
- Filesystem.
- Shell environment.
- Package manager.
- Process management.
- User accounts.
- Permissions.
- Environment variables.
- System services.
- Logs.
- Kernel configuration.
- Network interfaces.
- Storage management.
- Resource monitoring.
- SSH.
- Cron jobs.
- System administration.


Support realistic Linux-inspired commands and syntax.


Include a functional Bash environment and Python execution environment.


Allow players to write and execute programs, install packages, create scripts, compile software, and automate tasks.


Create realistic terminal outputs, errors, permissions, execution times, and dependencies.


The operating system must have actual internal state.


Commands must modify that state rather than generate decorative terminal text.


3. MODERN CLOUD COMPUTING


Reproduce the architecture of modern cloud infrastructure.


Include:


- Virtual machines.
- Containers.
- Docker-like containerization.
- Kubernetes-style orchestration.
- Virtual private clouds.
- Load balancers.
- Object storage.
- Block storage.
- Distributed databases.
- Serverless computing.
- Auto-scaling.
- Cloud networking.
- Identity and access management.
- Infrastructure as code.
- Monitoring and logging.


Players can rent, purchase, configure, and operate infrastructure.


They can build their own hosting companies and compete against simulated cloud providers.


Infrastructure costs must be dynamic.


CPU, RAM, storage, bandwidth, geographic location, availability, and redundancy affect pricing and performance.


4. ADVANCED SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT


Implement a functional software development ecosystem.


Support:


- Python.
- JavaScript.
- TypeScript.
- C.
- C++.
- Rust.
- Go.
- SQL.
- HTML.
- CSS.
- Bash.
- WebAssembly.


Provide:


- Code editors.
- Compilers.
- Interpreters.
- Debuggers.
- Git repositories.
- Package registries.
- Dependency managers.
- Build systems.
- Automated tests.
- CI/CD pipelines.
- Deployment systems.
- Version control.


Allow players to create complete applications.


Applications must be capable of running on simulated servers and being accessed through the simulated internet.


Implement software dependency trees, version conflicts, build failures, package updates, and compatibility problems.


5. ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ECOSYSTEM


Create a realistic emerging AI economy.


Include:


- AI development companies.
- Model hosting providers.
- AI APIs.
- Autonomous AI agents.
- Local inference servers.
- GPU computing infrastructure.
- Training pipelines.
- Model repositories.
- Vector databases.
- Retrieval-augmented generation.
- AI-powered applications.
- Agent communication systems.


NPC organizations should use AI agents to perform selected tasks.


AI agents can:


- Maintain websites.
- Manage customer support.
- Develop software.
- Analyze technical information.
- Monitor infrastructure.
- Operate business services.
- Coordinate with other agents.


Give each agent a defined role, capabilities, permissions, memory, resource budget, and objectives.


AI agents must not magically know everything. Their knowledge depends on available data, tools, computing resources, and permissions.


6. AUTONOMOUS DIGITAL CIVILIZATION


Generate a large population of independently acting digital entities.


Include:


INDIVIDUALS:


- Programmers.
- System administrators.
- Students.
- Researchers.
- Entrepreneurs.
- Freelancers.
- Content creators.
- Security professionals.
- Hobbyists.


ORGANIZATIONS:


- Technology companies.
- Hosting providers.
- Software publishers.
- Telecommunications companies.
- Financial platforms.
- Universities.
- Research laboratories.
- Government institutions.
- Independent communities.


Every organization has:


- Employees.
- Financial resources.
- Infrastructure.
- Products.
- Customers.
- Business objectives.
- Management structures.
- Competitors.
- Technical capabilities.


Organizations can grow, fail, merge, recruit, launch products, and change strategies.


NPCs must remember their experiences and relationships.


7. THE REALISTIC WEB


Create an extensive simulated World Wide Web.


Generate interconnected websites with:


- Unique domain names.
- Different designs.
- Owners.
- Hosting providers.
- DNS records.
- SSL certificates.
- Databases.
- Backend services.
- APIs.
- User accounts.
- Content.
- Search indexing.


Create:


- Search engines.
- Social networks.
- Forums.
- Blogs.
- News platforms.
- Online marketplaces.
- Developer communities.
- Documentation websites.
- Corporate portals.
- Private services.
- Personal websites.


Websites should be genuinely interconnected.


The player can discover websites through search engines, links, communities, DNS records, and other legitimate information sources.


Websites can become popular, lose traffic, change ownership, disappear, or experience technical problems.


8. CYBERSECURITY AND DIGITAL DEFENSE


Build a technically realistic cybersecurity simulation.


Implement:


- Authentication.
- Passkeys and WebAuthn.
- Multi-factor authentication.
- OAuth and OpenID Connect.
- Role-based access control.
- Zero-trust architecture.
- TLS certificates.
- Encryption.
- Vulnerability management.
- Security auditing.
- Network segmentation.
- Intrusion detection.
- Security monitoring.
- Digital forensics.
- Incident response.
- Software composition analysis.
- Software bills of materials.
- Code signing.
- Secure development pipelines.


Include realistic defensive and offensive security research in an isolated fictional environment.


Simulate vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, security patches, detection systems, and incident investigations.


The player can become a professional penetration tester, security researcher, infrastructure defender, or security consultant.


Unauthorized activity can produce realistic consequences.


9. DIGITAL ECONOMY


Build an independently evolving internet economy.


Players can:


- Sell software.
- Develop websites.
- Rent servers.
- Offer hosting.
- Sell APIs.
- Provide technical support.
- Develop commercial applications.
- Operate subscription services.
- Build technology companies.
- Hire developers.
- Purchase infrastructure.
- Negotiate contracts.


Create realistic supply and demand.


Companies compete for customers.


Products receive reviews.


Businesses can fail.


New opportunities emerge through changes in technology and market conditions.


Allow players to become wealthy through legitimate technical entrepreneurship.


10. SOCIAL INTERNET


Create an independent social environment.


Include:


- Email.
- Instant messaging.
- Public forums.
- Developer communities.
- Professional networks.
- Chat servers.
- Social media.
- Private groups.
- Digital identities.
- Reputation systems.


NPCs should communicate independently.


Players can build friendships, professional relationships, partnerships, and rivalries.


Other individuals can discover the player's projects and contact them.


11. ADVANCED NETWORK TOPOLOGY


Create an interactive representation of the simulated internet.


Display:


- Autonomous systems.
- Network connections.
- IP ranges.
- Routers.
- Gateways.
- Data centers.
- DNS infrastructure.
- Hosting providers.
- Geographic infrastructure.
- Network latency.
- Bandwidth.
- Packet loss.
- Routing changes.


Allow players to inspect networks at different levels.


Network maps must reflect actual simulated infrastructure and not random decorative connections.


12. REALISTIC ECONOMIC AND TECHNICAL EVENTS


Generate autonomous world events.


Examples:


- A cloud provider experiences an outage.
- A major website launches.
- A software framework receives a new release.
- A company hires developers.
- A hosting company changes its prices.
- A DNS configuration causes a service outage.
- A network experiences congestion.
- A security vulnerability is disclosed.
- A data center performs maintenance.
- A new AI service enters the market.
- A popular application experiences explosive growth.


Events should affect the economy and infrastructure.


13. PERSISTENCE AND WORLD HISTORY


The world must continue evolving while the player is offline.


Maintain persistent records of:


- NPC activities.
- Business operations.
- Financial transactions.
- Infrastructure changes.
- Software versions.
- Website ownership.
- Network topology.
- Social relationships.
- Market conditions.
- Security incidents.


When the player returns, provide a chronological activity report.


Allow the player to inspect historical events and investigate changes.


The simulation must support long-term saves and recoverable world states.


14. REALISTIC PLAYER LIFE


The player has an actual digital identity.


They have:


- A personal computer.
- An operating system.
- A home internet connection.
- Digital accounts.
- Email.
- Financial resources.
- Personal files.
- Software projects.
- Online relationships.
- Technical reputation.


The player can upgrade their hardware, purchase additional machines, establish a home laboratory, rent remote servers, and build an entire digital infrastructure.


Their decisions have long-term consequences.


15. GAMEPLAY FREEDOM


There must be no mandatory mission structure.


Do not force the player into predefined career paths.


The player can:


- Study networking.
- Learn programming.
- Build software.
- Explore the internet.
- Operate a company.
- Maintain infrastructure.
- Participate in communities.
- Research cybersecurity.
- Create digital services.
- Manage servers.
- Become an entrepreneur.


Progression must emerge from the player's actions.


16. TECHNICAL IMPLEMENTATION REQUIREMENTS


Build this as a complete, playable simulation rather than a static interface.


Use a modular architecture.


Recommended subsystems:


1. Virtual operating system.
2. Command interpreter.
3. Virtual filesystem.
4. Programming runtime.
5. Virtual network stack.
6. DNS and routing simulation.
7. Web server simulation.
8. Cloud infrastructure simulation.
9. NPC behavior engine.
10. AI agent simulation.
11. Economic simulation.
12. Social interaction engine.
13. Persistent database.
14. Event simulation engine.
15. Security simulation.
16. World-state manager.


Separate simulation logic from visual presentation.


Use deterministic simulation where appropriate.


Use event-driven updates and background processing.


Implement efficient save systems, world-state serialization, and incremental simulation.


Do not simulate every individual packet or every NPC continuously if it would make the game unplayable. Use different simulation detail levels depending on importance and player interaction.


17. DEVELOPMENT PRIORITIES


The complete vision is ambitious. Build it as an integrated game with progressively implemented systems.


First establish a genuinely functional core:


- A working terminal.
- A persistent computer.
- A virtual filesystem.
- Real command parsing.
- Functional programming execution.
- A simulated network.
- DNS resolution.
- Functional websites.
- Persistent NPCs.
- An evolving economy.


Then expand the same architecture with cloud infrastructure, advanced networking, AI agents, cybersecurity, and large-scale digital civilization.


Do not replace existing working systems when expanding the game.


All modules must integrate with the same persistent world.


FINAL REQUIREMENT


The result must feel like an actual digital world.


Not a hacking minigame.
Not a collection of scripted missions.
Not a fake terminal with random outputs.
Not a static collection of menus.


Build an internet civilization that the player can inhabit indefinitely.


The player should be able to start with one computer and eventually build a major technology company, operate a network infrastructure, develop widely used software, or simply live an independent digital life.


The internet must feel bigger than the player.


The world must never revolve exclusively around the player.


THE GAME IS NOT ABOUT HACKING THE INTERNET. IT IS ABOUT LIVING INSIDE A SIMULATED INTERNET.

## Objective
- Build “INTERNET: PERSISTENT WORLD,” a persistent browser-based internet civilization simulation centered on an authentic terminal workstation, and continue validating its existing systems.

## Requirements
- Create a functional, persistent simulation spanning terminal/OS, networking, web, cloud, software, autonomous entities, economy, social systems, security, and offline world evolution.
- Preserve the existing working systems and deterministic architecture; keep the fictional network isolated and consequential for unauthorized activity.
- No mandatory mission structure; support independent technical, commercial, infrastructure, and community-focused play.

## Decisions
- Use a static single-page browser application with modular JavaScript and a `WORLD_VERSION = 4` save compatibility layer.
- Keep the terminal primary within a professional workstation interface.

## Work State
### Completed
- Implemented workstation UI, persistent simulation, terminal command system, local storage, offline simulation/reporting, and workstation applications.
- JavaScript syntax checks passed for `src/util.js`, `src/data.js`, `src/vfs.js`, `src/world.js`, `src/shell.js`, and `src/main.js`.
- Served and loaded the app at `http://127.0.0.1:4173/`; exercised core commands and confirmed starter state, package availability, and terminal rendering.
- Began a follow-up validation pass; inspected offline-report logic and terminal handlers for `python3`, `gcc`, Git, and SQLite. No code changes made in that pass.

### Active
- Validate contract acceptance/submission, deployment, SSH, Git, Python/C, SQLite, browser navigation, mail, process termination, offline reports, and save/reload behavior.
- Investigate whether `gcc --version` incorrectly returns `gcc: fatal error: no input files`.
- Review repository status and diff after validation.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Continue browser checks at `http://127.0.0.1:4173/` for safe contract and infrastructure workflows.
2. Seed a save with an old `lastSaved`, reload, and verify offline report content and dismissal.
3. Exercise remaining workflows, monitor browser errors, and repeat tick/save/reload checks.
4. Inspect repository status and diff; investigate the `gcc --version` output.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Application entry point.
- `styles.css`: Workstation visual system.
- `src/main.js`: Persistence, UI, offline report, and world loop.
- `src/shell.js`: Terminal parser and command implementations.
- `src/world.js`: World generation, contracts, ticking, persistence revival, and offline simulation.
- `src/vfs.js`: Virtual filesystem and serialization.
- `src/data.js`: World entities and narrative data.
- `src/util.js`: Shared utilities and RNG.
- `src/systems.js`: Integrated simulation systems.

## Important Context
- `window.INTERNET` exposes app state; terminal is available as `window.INTERNET.windows.get('terminal').term`.
- Save key: `internet-persistent-world.v1`; previously observed save size approximately 551 KB.
- Starter state: `$1,840`, reputation `8`, heat `0%`, skill `1 (novice)`, cycle `001`, host `voidbox`, 19 open contracts, no owned servers/domains.
- Packages include `gcc`, `python3`, `git`, and `sqlite3`; `gcc --version` previously produced `gcc: fatal error: no input files`.
- Prior browser checks reported no application runtime errors; no changes were made during validation.

## Objective
- Build “INTERNET: PERSISTENT WORLD,” a persistent browser-based internet civilization simulation centered on an authentic terminal workstation, and validate its existing systems.

## Requirements
- Preserve working systems and deterministic architecture; keep the fictional network isolated and consequential for unauthorized activity.
- Support independent technical, commercial, infrastructure, and community-focused play without mandatory missions.
- Build an integrated, persistent simulation of the OS, networks, web, cloud, software, autonomous entities, economy, social systems, security, and offline world evolution.

## Decisions
- Use a static single-page browser application with modular JavaScript and `WORLD_VERSION = 4` save compatibility.
- Keep the terminal primary within a professional workstation interface.

## Work State
### Completed
- Implemented workstation UI, persistent simulation, terminal command system, local storage, offline simulation/reporting, and workstation applications.
- JavaScript syntax checks passed for `src/util.js`, `src/data.js`, `src/vfs.js`, `src/world.js`, `src/shell.js`, and `src/main.js`.
- Loaded the app at `http://127.0.0.1:4173/`; confirmed starter state, package availability, and terminal rendering.
- Confirmed browser app state and an existing offline report; no browser test commands have yet been successfully run through the terminal API.
- Inspected offline report logic and Python, GCC, Git, and SQLite handlers; no code changes made during the validation pass.

### Active
- Identify the terminal input/command submission path and continue safe workflow validation: contracts, deployment, SSH, Git, Python/C, SQLite, browser navigation, mail, process termination, offline reports, and save/reload.
- Investigate whether `gcc --version` incorrectly returns `gcc: fatal error: no input files`.
- Review repository status and diff after validation.

### Blocked
- Browser terminal commands cannot be invoked using the assumed `term.run` method; the terminal object exposes `print` and `clear`, plus input/queue state, but no command execution method.

## Next Move
1. Inspect terminal event handlers or command queue in `src/main.js`/`src/shell.js` and use the actual UI input path for command tests.
2. Run safe contracts and infrastructure workflows, then validate offline report creation/dismissal and save/reload behavior.
3. Check browser errors and tick/save/reload behavior; inspect `gcc --version`.
4. Review `git status` and diff; preserve existing uncommitted changes.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Application entry point.
- `styles.css`: Workstation visual system.
- `src/main.js`: Persistence, UI, offline report, and world loop.
- `src/shell.js`: Terminal parser and command implementations.
- `src/world.js`: World generation, contracts, ticking, persistence revival, and offline simulation.
- `src/vfs.js`: Virtual filesystem and serialization.
- `src/data.js`: World entities and narrative data.
- `src/util.js`: Shared utilities and RNG.
- `src/systems.js`: Integrated simulation systems.

## Important Context
- Existing work is uncommitted: modified `index.html`, `src/data.js`, `src/main.js`, `src/shell.js`, `src/world.js`, `styles.css`; untracked `src/systems.js`.
- Browser DevTools endpoint is available at port `9223`; app at `http://127.0.0.1:4173/`.
- `window.INTERNET` exposes app state; terminal window is `window.INTERNET.windows.get('terminal')`, with `term` fields `localFS`, `cwd`, `history`, `remote`, `user`, `host`, `env`, `queue`, `busy`, `input`, `print`, and `clear`.
- Save key: `internet-persistent-world.v1`; current observed save size approximately 1.19 MB.
- Observed state included cycle `12521`, money `$1,283`, reputation `8`, heat `0`, 27 open contracts, 2 owned servers, and an offline report for 540 real minutes / 10,080 world minutes.
- `gcc --version` previously produced `gcc: fatal error: no input files`; packages include `gcc`, `python3`, `git`, and `sqlite3`.

INTERNET: PERSISTENT WORLD

ULTIMATE INTERNET SIMULATION — 2026 EDITION


THE VISION


Create an extraordinarily realistic, terminal-driven internet civilization simulator.


The player must feel as though they own and operate an actual computer connected to a living, evolving global internet.


The game must simulate the modern internet as a complex interconnected ecosystem of infrastructure, people, organizations, software, protocols, services, businesses, artificial intelligence, and digital communities.


This is a persistent sandbox with no mandatory storyline.


The player is not a superhero hacker. They are an ordinary individual entering a complex digital society.


Their identity, reputation, resources, skills, relationships, business interests, and technical infrastructure evolve naturally.


The game should prioritize simulation depth, technical authenticity, freedom, and emergent gameplay.


1. MODERN INTERNET ARCHITECTURE


Recreate the actual structure of the modern internet.


Include multiple interconnected layers:


PHYSICAL INFRASTRUCTURE:


- Fiber-optic networks.
- Submarine communication cables.
- Internet exchange points.
- Data centers.
- Telecommunications infrastructure.
- Cellular networks.
- Wi-Fi networks.
- Routers and switches.
- Residential internet connections.
- Satellite connectivity.


NETWORK INFRASTRUCTURE:


- IPv4 and IPv6.
- TCP and UDP.
- QUIC.
- HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.
- DNS and DNSSEC.
- DHCP.
- NAT.
- BGP and autonomous systems.
- RPKI.
- VPN infrastructure.
- Proxies.
- Reverse proxies.
- Network address management.
- Routing tables.
- Firewalls.


WEB INFRASTRUCTURE:


- HTML.
- CSS.
- JavaScript.
- Web APIs.
- REST APIs.
- GraphQL.
- WebSockets.
- WebTransport.
- WebRTC.
- TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3.
- Certificates and public key infrastructure.
- CDNs.
- Caching systems.


All technologies must have functional implementations within the simulated environment.


Different protocols should have distinct characteristics, compatibility requirements, security implications, and performance consequences.


2. COMPLETE OPERATING SYSTEM SIMULATION


The player's computer should function like a real Linux workstation.


Provide:


- Terminal emulator.
- Filesystem.
- Shell environment.
- Package manager.
- Process management.
- User accounts.
- Permissions.
- Environment variables.
- System services.
- Logs.
- Kernel configuration.
- Network interfaces.
- Storage management.
- Resource monitoring.
- SSH.
- Cron jobs.
- System administration.


Support realistic Linux-inspired commands and syntax.


Include a functional Bash environment and Python execution environment.


Allow players to write and execute programs, install packages, create scripts, compile software, and automate tasks.


Create realistic terminal outputs, errors, permissions, execution times, and dependencies.


The operating system must have actual internal state.


Commands must modify that state rather than generate decorative terminal text.


3. MODERN CLOUD COMPUTING


Reproduce the architecture of modern cloud infrastructure.


Include:


- Virtual machines.
- Containers.
- Docker-like containerization.
- Kubernetes-style orchestration.
- Virtual private clouds.
- Load balancers.
- Object storage.
- Block storage.
- Distributed databases.
- Serverless computing.
- Auto-scaling.
- Cloud networking.
- Identity and access management.
- Infrastructure as code.
- Monitoring and logging.


Players can rent, purchase, configure, and operate infrastructure.


They can build their own hosting companies and compete against simulated cloud providers.


Infrastructure costs must be dynamic.


CPU, RAM, storage, bandwidth, geographic location, availability, and redundancy affect pricing and performance.


4. ADVANCED SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT


Implement a functional software development ecosystem.


Support:


- Python.
- JavaScript.
- TypeScript.
- C.
- C++.
- Rust.
- Go.
- SQL.
- HTML.
- CSS.
- Bash.
- WebAssembly.


Provide:


- Code editors.
- Compilers.
- Interpreters.
- Debuggers.
- Git repositories.
- Package registries.
- Dependency managers.
- Build systems.
- Automated tests.
- CI/CD pipelines.
- Deployment systems.
- Version control.


Allow players to create complete applications.


Applications must be capable of running on simulated servers and being accessed through the simulated internet.


Implement software dependency trees, version conflicts, build failures, package updates, and compatibility problems.


5. ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ECOSYSTEM


Create a realistic emerging AI economy.


Include:


- AI development companies.
- Model hosting providers.
- AI APIs.
- Autonomous AI agents.
- Local inference servers.
- GPU computing infrastructure.
- Training pipelines.
- Model repositories.
- Vector databases.
- Retrieval-augmented generation.
- AI-powered applications.
- Agent communication systems.


NPC organizations should use AI agents to perform selected tasks.


AI agents can:


- Maintain websites.
- Manage customer support.
- Develop software.
- Analyze technical information.
- Monitor infrastructure.
- Operate business services.
- Coordinate with other agents.


Give each agent a defined role, capabilities, permissions, memory, resource budget, and objectives.


AI agents must not magically know everything. Their knowledge depends on available data, tools, computing resources, and permissions.


6. AUTONOMOUS DIGITAL CIVILIZATION


Generate a large population of independently acting digital entities.


Include:


INDIVIDUALS:


- Programmers.
- System administrators.
- Students.
- Researchers.
- Entrepreneurs.
- Freelancers.
- Content creators.
- Security professionals.
- Hobbyists.


ORGANIZATIONS:


- Technology companies.
- Hosting providers.
- Software publishers.
- Telecommunications companies.
- Financial platforms.
- Universities.
- Research laboratories.
- Government institutions.
- Independent communities.


Every organization has:


- Employees.
- Financial resources.
- Infrastructure.
- Products.
- Customers.
- Business objectives.
- Management structures.
- Competitors.
- Technical capabilities.


Organizations can grow, fail, merge, recruit, launch products, and change strategies.


NPCs must remember their experiences and relationships.


7. THE REALISTIC WEB


Create an extensive simulated World Wide Web.


Generate interconnected websites with:


- Unique domain names.
- Different designs.
- Owners.
- Hosting providers.
- DNS records.
- SSL certificates.
- Databases.
- Backend services.
- APIs.
- User accounts.
- Content.
- Search indexing.


Create:


- Search engines.
- Social networks.
- Forums.
- Blogs.
- News platforms.
- Online marketplaces.
- Developer communities.
- Documentation websites.
- Corporate portals.
- Private services.
- Personal websites.


Websites should be genuinely interconnected.


The player can discover websites through search engines, links, communities, DNS records, and other legitimate information sources.


Websites can become popular, lose traffic, change ownership, disappear, or experience technical problems.


8. CYBERSECURITY AND DIGITAL DEFENSE


Build a technically realistic cybersecurity simulation.


Implement:


- Authentication.
- Passkeys and WebAuthn.
- Multi-factor authentication.
- OAuth and OpenID Connect.
- Role-based access control.
- Zero-trust architecture.
- TLS certificates.
- Encryption.
- Vulnerability management.
- Security auditing.
- Network segmentation.
- Intrusion detection.
- Security monitoring.
- Digital forensics.
- Incident response.
- Software composition analysis.
- Software bills of materials.
- Code signing.
- Secure development pipelines.


Include realistic defensive and offensive security research in an isolated fictional environment.


Simulate vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, security patches, detection systems, and incident investigations.


The player can become a professional penetration tester, security researcher, infrastructure defender, or security consultant.


Unauthorized activity can produce realistic consequences.


9. DIGITAL ECONOMY


Build an independently evolving internet economy.


Players can:


- Sell software.
- Develop websites.
- Rent servers.
- Offer hosting.
- Sell APIs.
- Provide technical support.
- Develop commercial applications.
- Operate subscription services.
- Build technology companies.
- Hire developers.
- Purchase infrastructure.
- Negotiate contracts.


Create realistic supply and demand.


Companies compete for customers.


Products receive reviews.


Businesses can fail.


New opportunities emerge through changes in technology and market conditions.


Allow players to become wealthy through legitimate technical entrepreneurship.


10. SOCIAL INTERNET


Create an independent social environment.


Include:


- Email.
- Instant messaging.
- Public forums.
- Developer communities.
- Professional networks.
- Chat servers.
- Social media.
- Private groups.
- Digital identities.
- Reputation systems.


NPCs should communicate independently.


Players can build friendships, professional relationships, partnerships, and rivalries.


Other individuals can discover the player's projects and contact them.


11. ADVANCED NETWORK TOPOLOGY


Create an interactive representation of the simulated internet.


Display:


- Autonomous systems.
- Network connections.
- IP ranges.
- Routers.
- Gateways.
- Data centers.
- DNS infrastructure.
- Hosting providers.
- Geographic infrastructure.
- Network latency.
- Bandwidth.
- Packet loss.
- Routing changes.


Allow players to inspect networks at different levels.


Network maps must reflect actual simulated infrastructure and not random decorative connections.


12. REALISTIC ECONOMIC AND TECHNICAL EVENTS


Generate autonomous world events.


Examples:


- A cloud provider experiences an outage.
- A major website launches.
- A software framework receives a new release.
- A company hires developers.
- A hosting company changes its prices.
- A DNS configuration causes a service outage.
- A network experiences congestion.
- A security vulnerability is disclosed.
- A data center performs maintenance.
- A new AI service enters the market.
- A popular application experiences explosive growth.


Events should affect the economy and infrastructure.


13. PERSISTENCE AND WORLD HISTORY


The world must continue evolving while the player is offline.


Maintain persistent records of:


- NPC activities.
- Business operations.
- Financial transactions.
- Infrastructure changes.
- Software versions.
- Website ownership.
- Network topology.
- Social relationships.
- Market conditions.
- Security incidents.


When the player returns, provide a chronological activity report.


Allow the player to inspect historical events and investigate changes.


The simulation must support long-term saves and recoverable world states.


14. REALISTIC PLAYER LIFE


The player has an actual digital identity.


They have:


- A personal computer.
- An operating system.
- A home internet connection.
- Digital accounts.
- Email.
- Financial resources.
- Personal files.
- Software projects.
- Online relationships.
- Technical reputation.


The player can upgrade their hardware, purchase additional machines, establish a home laboratory, rent remote servers, and build an entire digital infrastructure.


Their decisions have long-term consequences.


15. GAMEPLAY FREEDOM


There must be no mandatory mission structure.


Do not force the player into predefined career paths.


The player can:


- Study networking.
- Learn programming.
- Build software.
- Explore the internet.
- Operate a company.
- Maintain infrastructure.
- Participate in communities.
- Research cybersecurity.
- Create digital services.
- Manage servers.
- Become an entrepreneur.


Progression must emerge from the player's actions.


16. TECHNICAL IMPLEMENTATION REQUIREMENTS


Build this as a complete, playable simulation rather than a static interface.


Use a modular architecture.


Recommended subsystems:


1. Virtual operating system.
2. Command interpreter.
3. Virtual filesystem.
4. Programming runtime.
5. Virtual network stack.
6. DNS and routing simulation.
7. Web server simulation.
8. Cloud infrastructure simulation.
9. NPC behavior engine.
10. AI agent simulation.
11. Economic simulation.
12. Social interaction engine.
13. Persistent database.
14. Event simulation engine.
15. Security simulation.
16. World-state manager.


Separate simulation logic from visual presentation.


Use deterministic simulation where appropriate.


Use event-driven updates and background processing.


Implement efficient save systems, world-state serialization, and incremental simulation.


Do not simulate every individual packet or every NPC continuously if it would make the game unplayable. Use different simulation detail levels depending on importance and player interaction.


17. DEVELOPMENT PRIORITIES


The complete vision is ambitious. Build it as an integrated game with progressively implemented systems.


First establish a genuinely functional core:


- A working terminal.
- A persistent computer.
- A virtual filesystem.
- Real command parsing.
- Functional programming execution.
- A simulated network.
- DNS resolution.
- Functional websites.
- Persistent NPCs.
- An evolving economy.


Then expand the same architecture with cloud infrastructure, advanced networking, AI agents, cybersecurity, and large-scale digital civilization.


Do not replace existing working systems when expanding the game.


All modules must integrate with the same persistent world.


FINAL REQUIREMENT


The result must feel like an actual digital world.


Not a hacking minigame.
Not a collection of scripted missions.
Not a fake terminal with random outputs.
Not a static collection of menus.


Build an internet civilization that the player can inhabit indefinitely.


The player should be able to start with one computer and eventually build a major technology company, operate a network infrastructure, develop widely used software, or simply live an independent digital life.


The internet must feel bigger than the player.


The world must never revolve exclusively around the player.


THE GAME IS NOT ABOUT HACKING THE INTERNET. IT IS ABOUT LIVING INSIDE A SIMULATED INTERNET.

- Routers.
- Gateways.
- Data centers.
- DNS infrastructure.
- Hosting providers.
- Geographic infrastructure.
- Network latency.
- Bandwidth.
- Packet loss.
- Routing changes.


Allow players to inspect networks at different levels.


Network maps must reflect actual simulated infrastructure and not random decorative connections.


12. REALISTIC ECONOMIC AND TECHNICAL EVENTS


Generate autonomous world events.


Examples:


- A cloud provider experiences an outage.
- A major website launches.
- A software framework receives a new release.
- A company hires developers.
- A hosting company changes its prices.
- A DNS configuration causes a service outage.
- A network experiences congestion.
- A security vulnerability is disclosed.
- A data center performs maintenance.
- A new AI service enters the market.
- A popular application experiences explosive growth.


Events should affect the economy and infrastructure.


13. PERSISTENCE AND WORLD HISTORY


The world must continue evolving while the player is offline.


Maintain persistent records of:


- NPC activities.
- Business operations.
- Financial transactions.
- Infrastructure changes.
- Software versions.
- Website ownership.
- Network topology.
- Social relationships.
- Market conditions.
- Security incidents.


When the player returns, provide a chronological activity report.


Allow the player to inspect historical events and investigate changes.


The simulation must support long-term saves and recoverable world states.


14. REALISTIC PLAYER LIFE


The player has an actual digital identity.


They have:


- A personal computer.
- An operating system.
- A home internet connection.
- Digital accounts.
- Email.
- Financial resources.
- Personal files.
- Software projects.
- Online relationships.
- Technical reputation.


The player can upgrade their hardware, purchase additional machines, establish a home laboratory, rent remote servers, and build an entire digital infrastructure.


Their decisions have long-term consequences.


15. GAMEPLAY FREEDOM


There must be no mandatory mission structure.


Do not force the player into predefined career paths.


The player can:


- Study networking.
- Learn programming.
- Build software.
- Explore the internet.
- Operate a company.
- Maintain infrastructure.
- Participate in communities.
- Research cybersecurity.
- Create digital services.
- Manage servers.
- Become an entrepreneur.


Progression must emerge from the player's actions.


16. TECHNICAL IMPLEMENTATION REQUIREMENTS


Build this as a complete, playable simulation rather than a static interface.


Use a modular architecture.


Recommended subsystems:


1. Virtual operating system.
2. Command interpreter.
3. Virtual filesystem.
4. Programming runtime.
5. Virtual network stack.
6. DNS and routing simulation.
7. Web server simulation.
8. Cloud infrastructure simulation.
9. NPC behavior engine.
10. AI agent simulation.
11. Economic simulation.
12. Social interaction engine.
13. Persistent database.
14. Event simulation engine.
15. Security simulation.
16. World-state manager.


Separate simulation logic from visual presentation.


Use deterministic simulation where appropriate.


Use event-driven updates and background processing.


Implement efficient save systems, world-state serialization, and incremental simulation.


Do not simulate every individual packet or every NPC continuously if it would make the game unplayable. Use different simulation detail levels depending on importance and player interaction.


17. DEVELOPMENT PRIORITIES


The complete vision is ambitious. Build it as an integrated game with progressively implemented systems.


First establish a genuinely functional core:


- A working terminal.
- A persistent computer.
- A virtual filesystem.
- Real command parsing.
- Functional programming execution.
- A simulated network.
- DNS resolution.
- Functional websites.
- Persistent NPCs.
- An evolving economy.


Then expand the same architecture with cloud infrastructure, advanced networking, AI agents, cybersecurity, and large-scale digital civilization.


Do not replace existing working systems when expanding the game.


All modules must integrate with the same persistent world.


FINAL REQUIREMENT


The result must feel like an actual digital world.


Not a hacking minigame.
Not a collection of scripted missions.
Not a fake terminal with random outputs.
Not a static collection of menus.


Build an internet civilization that the player can inhabit indefinitely.


The player should be able to start with one computer and eventually build a major technology company, operate a network infrastructure, develop widely used software, or simply live an independent digital life.


The internet must feel bigger than the player.


The world must never revolve exclusively around the player.


THE GAME IS NOT ABOUT HACKING THE INTERNET. IT IS ABOUT LIVING INSIDE A SIMULATED INTERNET.

INTERNET: PERSISTENT WORLD

ULTIMATE INTERNET SIMULATION — 2026 EDITION

THE VISION

Create an extraordinarily realistic, terminal-driven internet civilization simulator.

The player must feel as though they own and operate an actual computer connected to a living, evolving global internet.

The game must simulate the modern internet as a complex interconnected ecosystem of infrastructure, people, organizations, software, protocols, services, businesses, artificial intelligence, and digital communities.

This is a persistent sandbox with no mandatory storyline.

The player is not a superhero hacker. They are an ordinary individual entering a complex digital society.

Their identity, reputation, resources, skills, relationships, business interests, and technical infrastructure evolve naturally.

The game should prioritize simulation depth, technical authenticity, freedom, and emergent gameplay.

1. MODERN INTERNET ARCHITECTURE

Recreate the actual structure of the modern internet.

Include multiple interconnected layers:

PHYSICAL INFRASTRUCTURE:

- Fiber-optic networks.
- Submarine communication cables.
- Internet exchange points.
- Data centers.
- Telecommunications infrastructure.
- Cellular networks.
- Wi-Fi networks.
- Routers and switches.
- Residential internet connections.
- Satellite connectivity.

NETWORK INFRASTRUCTURE:

- IPv4 and IPv6.
- TCP and UDP.
- QUIC.
- HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.
- DNS and DNSSEC.
- DHCP.
- NAT.
- BGP and autonomous systems.
- RPKI.
- VPN infrastructure.
- Proxies.
- Reverse proxies.
- Network address management.
- Routing tables.
- Firewalls.

WEB INFRASTRUCTURE:

- HTML.
- CSS.
- JavaScript.
- Web APIs.
- REST APIs.
- GraphQL.
- WebSockets.
- WebTransport.
- WebRTC.
- TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3.
- Certificates and public key infrastructure.
- CDNs.
- Caching systems.

All technologies must have functional implementations within the simulated environment.

Different protocols should have distinct characteristics, compatibility requirements, security implications, and performance consequences.

2. COMPLETE OPERATING SYSTEM SIMULATION

The player's computer should function like a real Linux workstation.

Provide:

- Terminal emulator.
- Filesystem.
- Shell environment.
- Package manager.
- Process management.
- User accounts.
- Permissions.
- Environment variables.
- System services.
- Logs.
- Kernel configuration.
- Network interfaces.
- Storage management.
- Resource monitoring.
- SSH.
- Cron jobs.
- System administration.

Support realistic Linux-inspired commands and syntax.

Include a functional Bash environment and Python execution environment.

Allow players to write and execute programs, install packages, create scripts, compile software, and automate tasks.

Create realistic terminal outputs, errors, permissions, execution times, and dependencies.

The operating system must have actual internal state.

Commands must modify that state rather than generate decorative terminal text.

3. MODERN CLOUD COMPUTING

Reproduce the architecture of modern cloud infrastructure.

Include:

- Virtual machines.
- Containers.
- Docker-like containerization.
- Kubernetes-style orchestration.
- Virtual private clouds.
- Load balancers.
- Object storage.
- Block storage.
- Distributed databases.
- Serverless computing.
- Auto-scaling.
- Cloud networking.
- Identity and access management.
- Infrastructure as code.
- Monitoring and logging.

Players can rent, purchase, configure, and operate infrastructure.

They can build their own hosting companies and compete against simulated cloud providers.

Infrastructure costs must be dynamic.

CPU, RAM, storage, bandwidth, geographic location, availability, and redundancy affect pricing and performance.

4. ADVANCED SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT

Implement a functional software development ecosystem.

Support:

- Python.
- JavaScript.
- TypeScript.
- C.
- C++.
- Rust.
- Go.
- SQL.
- HTML.
- CSS.
- Bash.
- WebAssembly.

Provide:

- Code editors.
- Compilers.
- Interpreters.
- Debuggers.
- Git repositories.
- Package registries.
- Dependency managers.
- Build systems.
- Automated tests.
- CI/CD pipelines.
- Deployment systems.
- Version control.

Allow players to create complete applications.

Applications must be capable of running on simulated servers and being accessed through the simulated internet.

Implement software dependency trees, version conflicts, build failures, package updates, and compatibility problems.

5. ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ECOSYSTEM

Create a realistic emerging AI economy.

Include:

- AI development companies.
- Model hosting providers.
- AI APIs.
- Autonomous AI agents.
- Local inference servers.
- GPU computing infrastructure.
- Training pipelines.
- Model repositories.
- Vector databases.
- Retrieval-augmented generation.
- AI-powered applications.
- Agent communication systems.

NPC organizations should use AI agents to perform selected tasks.

AI agents can:

- Maintain websites.
- Manage customer support.
- Develop software.
- Analyze technical information.
- Monitor infrastructure.
- Operate business services.
- Coordinate with other agents.

Give each agent a defined role, capabilities, permissions, memory, resource budget, and objectives.

AI agents must not magically know everything. Their knowledge depends on available data, tools, computing resources, and permissions.

6. AUTONOMOUS DIGITAL CIVILIZATION

Generate a large population of independently acting digital entities.

Include:

INDIVIDUALS:

- Programmers.
- System administrators.
- Students.
- Researchers.
- Entrepreneurs.
- Freelancers.
- Content creators.
- Security professionals.
- Hobbyists.

ORGANIZATIONS:

- Technology companies.
- Hosting providers.
- Software publishers.
- Telecommunications companies.
- Financial platforms.
- Universities.
- Research laboratories.
- Government institutions.
- Independent communities.

Every organization has:

- Employees.
- Financial resources.
- Infrastructure.
- Products.
- Customers.
- Business objectives.
- Management structures.
- Competitors.
- Technical capabilities.

Organizations can grow, fail, merge, recruit, launch products, and change strategies.

NPCs must remember their experiences and relationships.

7. THE REALISTIC WEB

Create an extensive simulated World Wide Web.

Generate interconnected websites with:

- Unique domain names.
- Different designs.
- Owners.
- Hosting providers.
- DNS records.
- SSL certificates.
- Databases.
- Backend services.
- APIs.
- User accounts.
- Content.
- Search indexing.

Create:

- Search engines.
- Social networks.
- Forums.
- Blogs.
- News platforms.
- Online marketplaces.
- Developer communities.
- Documentation websites.
- Corporate portals.
- Private services.
- Personal websites.

Websites should be genuinely interconnected.

The player can discover websites through search engines, links, communities, DNS records, and other legitimate information sources.

Websites can become popular, lose traffic, change ownership, disappear, or experience technical problems.

8. CYBERSECURITY AND DIGITAL DEFENSE

Build a technically realistic cybersecurity simulation.

Implement:

- Authentication.
- Passkeys and WebAuthn.
- Multi-factor authentication.
- OAuth and OpenID Connect.
- Role-based access control.
- Zero-trust architecture.
- TLS certificates.
- Encryption.
- Vulnerability management.
- Security auditing.
- Network segmentation.
- Intrusion detection.
- Security monitoring.
- Digital forensics.
- Incident response.
- Software composition analysis.
- Software bills of materials.
- Code signing.
- Secure development pipelines.

Include realistic defensive and offensive security research in an isolated fictional environment.

Simulate vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, security patches, detection systems, and incident investigations.

The player can become a professional penetration tester, security researcher, infrastructure defender, or security consultant.

Unauthorized activity can produce realistic consequences.

9. DIGITAL ECONOMY

Build an independently evolving internet economy.

Players can:

- Sell software.
- Develop websites.
- Rent servers.
- Offer hosting.
- Sell APIs.
- Provide technical support.
- Develop commercial applications.
- Operate subscription services.
- Build technology companies.
- Hire developers.
- Purchase infrastructure.
- Negotiate contracts.

Create realistic supply and demand.

Companies compete for customers.

Products receive reviews.

Businesses can fail.

New opportunities emerge through changes in technology and market conditions.

Allow players to become wealthy through legitimate technical entrepreneurship.

10. SOCIAL INTERNET

Create an independent social environment.

Include:

- Email.
- Instant messaging.
- Public forums.
- Developer communities.
- Professional networks.
- Chat servers.
- Social media.
- Private groups.
- Digital identities.
- Reputation systems.

NPCs should communicate independently.

Players can build friendships, professional relationships, partnerships, and rivalries.

Other individuals can discover the player's projects and contact them.

11. ADVANCED NETWORK TOPOLOGY

Create an interactive representation of the simulated internet.

Display:

- Autonomous systems.
- Network connections.
- IP ranges.
- Routers.
- Gateways.
- Data centers.
- DNS infrastructure.
- Hosting providers.
- Geographic infrastructure.
- Network latency.
- Bandwidth.
- Packet loss.
- Routing changes.

Allow players to inspect networks at different levels.

Network maps must reflect actual simulated infrastructure and not random decorative connections.

12. REALISTIC ECONOMIC AND TECHNICAL EVENTS

Generate autonomous world events.

Examples:

- A cloud provider experiences an outage.
- A major website launches.
- A software framework receives a new release.
- A company hires developers.
- A hosting company changes its prices.
- A DNS configuration causes a service outage.
- A network experiences congestion.
- A security vulnerability is disclosed.
- A data center performs maintenance.
- A new AI service enters the market.
- A popular application experiences explosive growth.

Events should affect the economy and infrastructure.

13. PERSISTENCE AND WORLD HISTORY

The world must continue evolving while the player is offline.

Maintain persistent records of:

- NPC activities.
- Business operations.
- Financial transactions.
- Infrastructure changes.
- Software versions.
- Website ownership.
- Network topology.
- Social relationships.
- Market conditions.
- Security incidents.

When the player returns, provide a chronological activity report.

Allow the player to inspect historical events and investigate changes.

The simulation must support long-term saves and recoverable world states.

14. REALISTIC PLAYER LIFE

The player has an actual digital identity.

They have:

- A personal computer.
- An operating system.
- A home internet connection.
- Digital accounts.
- Email.
- Financial resources.
- Personal files.
- Software projects.
- Online relationships.
- Technical reputation.

The player can upgrade their hardware, purchase additional machines, establish a home laboratory, rent remote servers, and build an entire digital infrastructure.

Their decisions have long-term consequences.

15. GAMEPLAY FREEDOM

There must be no mandatory mission structure.

Do not force the player into predefined career paths.

The player can:

- Study networking.
- Learn programming.
- Build software.
- Explore the internet.
- Operate a company.
- Maintain infrastructure.
- Participate in communities.
- Research cybersecurity.
- Create digital services.
- Manage servers.
- Become an entrepreneur.

Progression must emerge from the player's actions.

16. TECHNICAL IMPLEMENTATION REQUIREMENTS

Build this as a complete, playable simulation rather than a static interface.

Use a modular architecture.

Recommended subsystems:

1. Virtual operating system.
2. Command interpreter.
3. Virtual filesystem.
4. Programming runtime.
5. Virtual network stack.
6. DNS and routing simulation.
7. Web server simulation.
8. Cloud infrastructure simulation.
9. NPC behavior engine.
10. AI agent simulation.
11. Economic simulation.
12. Social interaction engine.
13. Persistent database.
14. Event simulation engine.
15. Security simulation.
16. World-state manager.

Separate simulation logic from visual presentation.

Use deterministic simulation where appropriate.

Use event-driven updates and background processing.

Implement efficient save systems, world-state serialization, and incremental simulation.

Do not simulate every individual packet or every NPC continuously if it would make the game unplayable. Use different simulation detail levels depending on importance and player interaction.

17. DEVELOPMENT PRIORITIES

The complete vision is ambitious. Build it as an integrated game with progressively implemented systems.

First establish a genuinely functional core:

- A working terminal.
- A persistent computer.
- A virtual filesystem.
- Real command parsing.
- Functional programming execution.
- A simulated network.
- DNS resolution.
- Functional websites.
- Persistent NPCs.
- An evolving economy.

Then expand the same architecture with cloud infrastructure, advanced networking, AI agents, cybersecurity, and large-scale digital civilization.

Do not replace existing working systems when expanding the game.

All modules must integrate with the same persistent world.

FINAL REQUIREMENT

The result must feel like an actual digital world.

Not a hacking minigame.
Not a collection of scripted missions.
Not a fake terminal with random outputs.
Not a static collection of menus.

Build an internet civilization that the player can inhabit indefinitely.

The player should be able to start with one computer and eventually build a major technology company, operate a network infrastructure, develop widely used software, or simply live an independent digital life.

The internet must feel bigger than the player.

The world must never revolve exclusively around the player.

THE GAME IS NOT ABOUT HACKING THE INTERNET. IT IS ABOUT LIVING INSIDE A SIMULATED INTERNET.

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Continue developing “INTERNET: PERSISTENT WORLD,” an indefinitely playable, persistent internet civilization simulation.
- Expand and validate the integrated simulation while preserving its existing core and save compatibility.

## Requirements
- Preserve the terminal-driven sandbox, deterministic architecture where appropriate, and `WORLD_VERSION = 4` save compatibility.
- Build toward a functional OS, networking, web, cloud, software development, AI agents, autonomous entities, economy, social systems, security, and offline evolution.
- Keep the simulation isolated and fictional; unauthorized activity should have meaningful consequences.
- Support independent play without mandatory missions or career paths.
- Prioritize integrated functionality over decorative UI or command output.

## Decisions
- Use a static single-page browser application with modular JavaScript and a professional workstation interface centered on the terminal.
- Extend the existing shared persistent world and systems rather than replacing them.

## Work State
### Completed
- Implemented workstation UI, terminal, virtual filesystem, persistent world, simulation loop, offline report, and workstation applications.
- Fixed GCC version flag handling in `src/shell.js`.
- Updated `src/world.js` to process site revenue across every crossed 10-minute boundary and bill once per crossed world day, including multi-day ticks and v4 saves lacking `lastRentDay`.
- Verified tick boundary, large-chunk billing, legacy save revival, JavaScript syntax, and whitespace checks.

### Active
- Expand and validate integrated OS, network, web, cloud, NPC, economy, social, and security behavior.
- Validate browser interactions, save/reload, and offline reports.

### Blocked
- Browser CDP validation previously returned `undefined` for evaluated results; browser interaction and reload behavior remain unverified.

## Next Move
1. Continue browser checks for terminal commands, simulation changes, save/reload, and offline-report behavior.
2. Investigate remaining functional integration gaps across the broader civilization systems.

## Relevant Files
- `src/world.js`: World generation, ticking, persistence, offline simulation, and recent billing/revenue changes.
- `src/main.js`: UI, persistence, offline reports, world loop, and terminal input bridge.
- `src/systems.js`: Cloud, container, agent, and organization simulation helpers.
- `src/shell.js`: Command parser and simulated OS/tool commands.
- `src/vfs.js`: Virtual filesystem and serialization.
- `src/data.js`: World entities and narrative data.
- `index.html`: Application entry point.
- `styles.css`: Workstation interface.
- `src/util.js`: Shared utilities and deterministic RNG.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted: modified `index.html`, `src/data.js`, `src/main.js`, `src/shell.js`, `src/world.js`, `styles.css`; untracked `src/systems.js`.
- Regression checks passed using Node.js, including normal and large ticks, multiple crossed billing days, and legacy v4 save revival.
- The app responded at `http://127.0.0.1:4173/` with HTTP 200; save key is `internet-persistent-world.v1`.

metadata.displayText:
INTERNET: PERSISTENT WORLD

ULTIMATE INTERNET SIMULATION — 2026 EDITION

THE VISION

Create an extraordinarily realistic, terminal-driven internet civilization simulator.

The player must feel as though they own and operate an actual computer connected to a living, evolving global internet.

The game must simulate the modern internet as a complex interconnected ecosystem of infrastructure, people, organizations, software, protocols, services, businesses, artificial intelligence, and digital communities.

This is a persistent sandbox with no mandatory storyline.

The player is not a superhero hacker. They are an ordinary individual entering a complex digital society.

Their identity, reputation, resources, skills, relationships, business interests, and technical infrastructure evolve naturally.

The game should prioritize simulation depth, technical authenticity, freedom, and emergent gameplay.

1. MODERN INTERNET ARCHITECTURE

Recreate the actual structure of the modern internet.

Include multiple interconnected layers:

PHYSICAL INFRASTRUCTURE:

- Fiber-optic networks.
- Submarine communication cables.
- Internet exchange points.
- Data centers.
- Telecommunications infrastructure.
- Cellular networks.
- Wi-Fi networks.
- Routers and switches.
- Residential internet connections.
- Satellite connectivity.

NETWORK INFRASTRUCTURE:

- IPv4 and IPv6.
- TCP and UDP.
- QUIC.
- HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.
- DNS and DNSSEC.
- DHCP.
- NAT.
- BGP and autonomous systems.
- RPKI.
- VPN infrastructure.
- Proxies.
- Reverse proxies.
- Network address management.
- Routing tables.
- Firewalls.

WEB INFRASTRUCTURE:

- HTML.
- CSS.
- JavaScript.
- Web APIs.
- REST APIs.
- GraphQL.
- WebSockets.
- WebTransport.
- WebRTC.
- TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3.
- Certificates and public key infrastructure.
- CDNs.
- Caching systems.

All technologies must have functional implementations within the simulated environment.

Different protocols should have distinct characteristics, compatibility requirements, security implications, and performance consequences.

2. COMPLETE OPERATING SYSTEM SIMULATION

The player's computer should function like a real Linux workstation.

Provide:

- Terminal emulator.
- Filesystem.
- Shell environment.
- Package manager.
- Process management.
- User accounts.
- Permissions.
- Environment variables.
- System services.
- Logs.
- Kernel configuration.
- Network interfaces.
- Storage management.
- Resource monitoring.
- SSH.
- Cron jobs.
- System administration.

Support realistic Linux-inspired commands and syntax.

Include a functional Bash environment and Python execution environment.

Allow players to write and execute programs, install packages, create scripts, compile software, and automate tasks.

Create realistic terminal outputs, errors, permissions, execution times, and dependencies.

The operating system must have actual internal state.

Commands must modify that state rather than generate decorative terminal text.

3. MODERN CLOUD COMPUTING

Reproduce the architecture of modern cloud infrastructure.

Include:

- Virtual machines.
- Containers.
- Docker-like containerization.
- Kubernetes-style orchestration.
- Virtual private clouds.
- Load balancers.
- Object storage.

- A persistent computer.
- A virtual filesystem.
- Real command parsing.
- Functional programming execution.
- A simulated network.
- DNS resolution.
- Functional websites.
- Persistent NPCs.
- An evolving economy.

Not a static collection of menus.

INTERNET: PERSISTENT WORLD

ULTIMATE INTERNET SIMULATION — 2026 EDITION


THE VISION


Create an extraordinarily realistic, terminal-driven internet civilization simulator.


The player must feel as though they own and operate an actual computer connected to a living, evolving global internet.


The game must simulate the modern internet as a complex interconnected ecosystem of infrastructure, people, organizations, software, protocols, services, businesses, artificial intelligence, and digital communities.


This is a persistent sandbox with no mandatory storyline.


The player is not a superhero hacker. They are an ordinary individual entering a complex digital society.


Their identity, reputation, resources, skills, relationships, business interests, and technical infrastructure evolve naturally.


The game should prioritize simulation depth, technical authenticity, freedom, and emergent gameplay.


1. MODERN INTERNET ARCHITECTURE


Recreate the actual structure of the modern internet.


Include multiple interconnected layers:


PHYSICAL INFRASTRUCTURE:


- Fiber-optic networks.
- Submarine communication cables.
- Internet exchange points.
- Data centers.
- Telecommunications infrastructure.
- Cellular networks.
- Wi-Fi networks.
- Routers and switches.
- Residential internet connections.
- Satellite connectivity.


NETWORK INFRASTRUCTURE:


- IPv4 and IPv6.
- TCP and UDP.
- QUIC.
- HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.
- DNS and DNSSEC.
- DHCP.
- NAT.
- BGP and autonomous systems.
- RPKI.
- VPN infrastructure.
- Proxies.
- Reverse proxies.
- Network address management.
- Routing tables.
- Firewalls.


WEB INFRASTRUCTURE:


- HTML.
- CSS.
- JavaScript.
- Web APIs.
- REST APIs.
- GraphQL.
- WebSockets.
- WebTransport.
- WebRTC.
- TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3.
- Certificates and public key infrastructure.
- CDNs.
- Caching systems.


All technologies must have functional implementations within the simulated environment.


Different protocols should have distinct characteristics, compatibility requirements, security implications, and performance consequences.


2. COMPLETE OPERATING SYSTEM SIMULATION


The player's computer should function like a real Linux workstation.


Provide:


- Terminal emulator.
- Filesystem.
- Shell environment.
- Package manager.
- Process management.
- User accounts.
- Permissions.
- Environment variables.
- System services.
- Logs.
- Kernel configuration.
- Network interfaces.
- Storage management.
- Resource monitoring.
- SSH.
- Cron jobs.
- System administration.


Support realistic Linux-inspired commands and syntax.


Include a functional Bash environment and Python execution environment.


Allow players to write and execute programs, install packages, create scripts, compile software, and automate tasks.


Create realistic terminal outputs, errors, permissions, execution times, and dependencies.


The operating system must have actual internal state.


Commands must modify that state rather than generate decorative terminal text.


3. MODERN CLOUD COMPUTING


Reproduce the architecture of modern cloud infrastructure.


Include:


- Virtual machines.
- Containers.
- Docker-like containerization.
- Kubernetes-style orchestration.
- Virtual private clouds.
- Load balancers.
- Object storage.
- Block storage.
- Distributed databases.
- Serverless computing.
- Auto-scaling.
- Cloud networking.
- Identity and access management.
- Infrastructure as code.
- Monitoring and logging.


Players can rent, purchase, configure, and operate infrastructure.


They can build their own hosting companies and compete against simulated cloud providers.


Infrastructure costs must be dynamic.


CPU, RAM, storage, bandwidth, geographic location, availability, and redundancy affect pricing and performance.


4. ADVANCED SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT


Implement a functional software development ecosystem.


Support:


- Python.
- JavaScript.
- TypeScript.
- C.
- C++.
- Rust.
- Go.
- SQL.
- HTML.
- CSS.
- Bash.
- WebAssembly.


Provide:


- Code editors.
- Compilers.
- Interpreters.
- Debuggers.
- Git repositories.
- Package registries.
- Dependency managers.
- Build systems.
- Automated tests.
- CI/CD pipelines.
- Deployment systems.
- Version control.


Allow players to create complete applications.


Applications must be capable of running on simulated servers and being accessed through the simulated internet.


Implement software dependency trees, version conflicts, build failures, package updates, and compatibility problems.


5. ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ECOSYSTEM


Create a realistic emerging AI economy.


Include:


- AI development companies.
- Model hosting providers.
- AI APIs.
- Autonomous AI agents.
- Local inference servers.
- GPU computing infrastructure.
- Training pipelines.
- Model repositories.
- Vector databases.
- Retrieval-augmented generation.
- AI-powered applications.
- Agent communication systems.


NPC organizations should use AI agents to perform selected tasks.


AI agents can:


- Maintain websites.
- Manage customer support.
- Develop software.
- Analyze technical information.
- Monitor infrastructure.
- Operate business services.
- Coordinate with other agents.


Give each agent a defined role, capabilities, permissions, memory, resource budget, and objectives.


AI agents must not magically know everything. Their knowledge depends on available data, tools, computing resources, and permissions.


6. AUTONOMOUS DIGITAL CIVILIZATION


Generate a large population of independently acting digital entities.


Include:


INDIVIDUALS:


- Programmers.
- System administrators.
- Students.
- Researchers.
- Entrepreneurs.
- Freelancers.
- Content creators.
- Security professionals.
- Hobbyists.


ORGANIZATIONS:


- Technology companies.
- Hosting providers.
- Software publishers.
- Telecommunications companies.
- Financial platforms.
- Universities.
- Research laboratories.
- Government institutions.
- Independent communities.


Every organization has:


- Employees.
- Financial resources.
- Infrastructure.
- Products.
- Customers.
- Business objectives.
- Management structures.
- Competitors.
- Technical capabilities.


Organizations can grow, fail, merge, recruit, launch products, and change strategies.


NPCs must remember their experiences and relationships.


7. THE REALISTIC WEB


Create an extensive simulated World Wide Web.


Generate interconnected websites with:


- Unique domain names.
- Different designs.
- Owners.
- Hosting providers.
- DNS records.
- SSL certificates.
- Databases.
- Backend services.
- APIs.
- User accounts.
- Content.
- Search indexing.


Create:


- Search engines.
- Social networks.
- Forums.
- Blogs.
- News platforms.
- Online marketplaces.
- Developer communities.
- Documentation websites.
- Corporate portals.
- Private services.
- Personal websites.


Websites should be genuinely interconnected.


The player can discover websites through search engines, links, communities, DNS records, and other legitimate information sources.


Websites can become popular, lose traffic, change ownership, disappear, or experience technical problems.


8. CYBERSECURITY AND DIGITAL DEFENSE


Build a technically realistic cybersecurity simulation.


Implement:


- Authentication.
- Passkeys and WebAuthn.
- Multi-factor authentication.
- OAuth and OpenID Connect.
- Role-based access control.
- Zero-trust architecture.
- TLS certificates.
- Encryption.
- Vulnerability management.
- Security auditing.
- Network segmentation.
- Intrusion detection.
- Security monitoring.
- Digital forensics.
- Incident response.
- Software composition analysis.
- Software bills of materials.
- Code signing.
- Secure development pipelines.


Include realistic defensive and offensive security research in an isolated fictional environment.


Simulate vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, security patches, detection systems, and incident investigations.


The player can become a professional penetration tester, security researcher, infrastructure defender, or security consultant.


Unauthorized activity can produce realistic consequences.


9. DIGITAL ECONOMY


Build an independently evolving internet economy.


Players can:


- Sell software.
- Develop websites.
- Rent servers.
- Offer hosting.
- Sell APIs.
- Provide technical support.
- Develop commercial applications.
- Operate subscription services.
- Build technology companies.
- Hire developers.
- Purchase infrastructure.
- Negotiate contracts.


Create realistic supply and demand.


Companies compete for customers.


Products receive reviews.


Businesses can fail.


New opportunities emerge through changes in technology and market conditions.


Allow players to become wealthy through legitimate technical entrepreneurship.


10. SOCIAL INTERNET


Create an independent social environment.


Include:


- Email.
- Instant messaging.
- Public forums.
- Developer communities.
- Professional networks.
- Chat servers.
- Social media.
- Private groups.
- Digital identities.
- Reputation systems.


NPCs should communicate independently.


Players can build friendships, professional relationships, partnerships, and rivalries.


Other individuals can discover the player's projects and contact them.


11. ADVANCED NETWORK TOPOLOGY


Create an interactive representation of the simulated internet.


Display:


- Autonomous systems.
- Network connections.
- IP ranges.
- Routers.
- Gateways.
- Data centers.
- DNS infrastructure.
- Hosting providers.
- Geographic infrastructure.
- Network latency.
- Bandwidth.
- Packet loss.
- Routing changes.


Allow players to inspect networks at different levels.


Network maps must reflect actual simulated infrastructure and not random decorative connections.


12. REALISTIC ECONOMIC AND TECHNICAL EVENTS


Generate autonomous world events.


Examples:


- A cloud provider experiences an outage.
- A major website launches.
- A software framework receives a new release.
- A company hires developers.
- A hosting company changes its prices.
- A DNS configuration causes a service outage.
- A network experiences congestion.
- A security vulnerability is disclosed.
- A data center performs maintenance.
- A new AI service enters the market.
- A popular application experiences explosive growth.


Events should affect the economy and infrastructure.


13. PERSISTENCE AND WORLD HISTORY


The world must continue evolving while the player is offline.


Maintain persistent records of:


- NPC activities.
- Business operations.
- Financial transactions.
- Infrastructure changes.
- Software versions.
- Website ownership.
- Network topology.
- Social relationships.
- Market conditions.
- Security incidents.


When the player returns, provide a chronological activity report.


Allow the player to inspect historical events and investigate changes.


The simulation must support long-term saves and recoverable world states.


14. REALISTIC PLAYER LIFE


The player has an actual digital identity.


They have:


- A personal computer.
- An operating system.
- A home internet connection.
- Digital accounts.
- Email.
- Financial resources.
- Personal files.
- Software projects.
- Online relationships.
- Technical reputation.


The player can upgrade their hardware, purchase additional machines, establish a home laboratory, rent remote servers, and build an entire digital infrastructure.


Their decisions have long-term consequences.


15. GAMEPLAY FREEDOM


There must be no mandatory mission structure.


Do not force the player into predefined career paths.


The player can:


- Study networking.
- Learn programming.
- Build software.
- Explore the internet.
- Operate a company.
- Maintain infrastructure.
- Participate in communities.
- Research cybersecurity.
- Create digital services.
- Manage servers.
- Become an entrepreneur.


Progression must emerge from the player's actions.


16. TECHNICAL IMPLEMENTATION REQUIREMENTS


Build this as a complete, playable simulation rather than a static interface.


Use a modular architecture.


Recommended subsystems:


1. Virtual operating system.
2. Command interpreter.
3. Virtual filesystem.
4. Programming runtime.
5. Virtual network stack.
6. DNS and routing simulation.
7. Web server simulation.
8. Cloud infrastructure simulation.
9. NPC behavior engine.
10. AI agent simulation.
11. Economic simulation.
12. Social interaction engine.
13. Persistent database.
14. Event simulation engine.
15. Security simulation.
16. World-state manager.


Separate simulation logic from visual presentation.


Use deterministic simulation where appropriate.


Use event-driven updates and background processing.


Implement efficient save systems, world-state serialization, and incremental simulation.


Do not simulate every individual packet or every NPC continuously if it would make the game unplayable. Use different simulation detail levels depending on importance and player interaction.


17. DEVELOPMENT PRIORITIES


The complete vision is ambitious. Build it as an integrated game with progressively implemented systems.


First establish a genuinely functional core:


- A working terminal.
- A persistent computer.
- A virtual filesystem.
- Real command parsing.
- Functional programming execution.
- A simulated network.
- DNS resolution.
- Functional websites.
- Persistent NPCs.
- An evolving economy.


Then expand the same architecture with cloud infrastructure, advanced networking, AI agents, cybersecurity, and large-scale digital civilization.


Do not replace existing working systems when expanding the game.


All modules must integrate with the same persistent world.


FINAL REQUIREMENT


The result must feel like an actual digital world.


Not a hacking minigame.
Not a collection of scripted missions.
Not a fake terminal with random outputs.
Not a static collection of menus.


Build an internet civilization that the player can inhabit indefinitely.


The player should be able to start with one computer and eventually build a major technology company, operate a network infrastructure, develop widely used software, or simply live an independent digital life.


The internet must feel bigger than the player.


The world must never revolve exclusively around the player.


THE GAME IS NOT ABOUT HACKING THE INTERNET. IT IS ABOUT LIVING INSIDE A SIMULATED INTERNET.
