messages.text:
"INTERNET: PERSISTENT WORLD

ULTIMATE EXPANSION III — DIGITAL CIVILIZATION

Integrate the following systems into the existing game without removing or simplifying previously implemented features.

The objective is to create a comprehensive simulation of modern human civilization connected through a persistent digital ecosystem.

All systems must interact with the same world, economy, NPC population, databases, and historical timeline.

A. GLOBAL COUNTRIES AND GEOPOLITICS

Create a simulated world containing multiple countries and regions.

Each country has:

- Government.
- Political institutions.
- Economy.
- Currency.
- Population.
- Internet infrastructure.
- Telecommunications providers.
- Taxation system.
- Digital regulations.
- Financial institutions.
- Universities.
- Technology industries.

Simulate international relations, trade agreements, regulatory changes, technological competition, sanctions, diplomatic negotiations, and cyber policies.

Government decisions should affect businesses, individuals, investments, technology adoption, and internet accessibility.

B. LAW AND DIGITAL GOVERNANCE

Create an evolving legal system.

Include:

- Digital privacy laws.
- Intellectual property.
- Copyright.
- Software licensing.
- Business registration.
- Employment regulations.
- Financial regulations.
- Consumer protection.
- Cybercrime legislation.
- Data protection.
- Cryptocurrency regulations.
- Digital contracts.

NPC organizations and players must be subject to applicable simulated regulations.

Introduce courts, regulatory authorities, compliance departments, lawyers, investigators, and legal disputes.

Consequences must depend on the jurisdiction and circumstances.

C. COMPLETE EDUCATION SYSTEM

Create schools, colleges, universities, online learning platforms, and independent training institutions.

NPCs can:

- Study programming.
- Learn cybersecurity.
- Study finance.
- Learn mathematics.
- Research artificial intelligence.
- Obtain certifications.
- Attend university.
- Publish research.
- Become teachers.
- Develop professional expertise.

Players can independently study subjects through realistic documentation, tutorials, laboratories, programming challenges, and educational resources.

Knowledge should be transferable to practical gameplay.

D. SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH AND DISCOVERY

Create an autonomous research ecosystem.

Universities, corporations, independent researchers, and laboratories can pursue discoveries.

Research fields include:

- Computer science.
- Artificial intelligence.
- Robotics.
- Semiconductor engineering.
- Cryptography.
- Quantum computing.
- Telecommunications.
- Materials science.
- Energy technology.
- Biotechnology.

Discoveries must require research time, funding, equipment, expertise, and experimentation.

New technologies should influence the world economy and create new industries.

Do not randomly invent impossible technologies. Maintain plausible technological dependencies and development timelines.

E. MEDIA AND INFORMATION ECOSYSTEM

Create autonomous media organizations.

Include:

- Newspapers.
- Online magazines.
- Television networks.
- Independent journalists.
- Social media platforms.
- Streaming services.
- Video creators.
- Podcasts.
- Advertising agencies.
- Public relations companies.

NPCs can create content, build audiences, publish news, produce entertainment, and monetize their work.

Information spreads through social networks according to audience size, trust, relevance, and sharing behavior.

Simulate misinformation, corrections, investigative journalism, media competition, and public opinion.

F. PHYSICAL WORLD AND INFRASTRUCTURE

Expand the simulated world beyond the internet.

Create interconnected cities with:

- Residential areas.
- Commercial districts.
- Offices.
- Industrial zones.
- Universities.
- Hospitals.
- Data centers.
- Warehouses.
- Shops.
- Transportation networks.

Simulate electricity, telecommunications, water, transportation, logistics, and physical equipment.

Infrastructure failures should affect digital services.

A regional electricity outage could interrupt data centers.

A damaged fiber-optic connection could increase latency.

A shortage of semiconductor components could delay hardware production.

G. REAL ESTATE AND PROPERTY ECONOMY

Allow NPCs and players to acquire:

- Apartments.
- Houses.
- Offices.
- Commercial buildings.
- Industrial facilities.
- Data centers.
- Warehouses.
- Land.

Simulate rent, maintenance, mortgages, property taxes, construction, insurance, and real estate market fluctuations.

Businesses can purchase offices, expand facilities, and establish regional headquarters.

NPCs can move between properties based on employment, income, family circumstances, and preferences.

H. GLOBAL SUPPLY CHAINS

Create a complex production and distribution economy.

Businesses depend on suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, transportation providers, and customers.

Track:

- Raw materials.
- Components.
- Semiconductor availability.
- Hardware manufacturing.
- Inventory.
- Shipping.
- Warehousing.
- Energy costs.
- Production capacity.

Products must require actual resources and manufacturing processes within the simulation.

Supply shortages, transportation disruptions, and rising production costs should influence market prices and company profitability.

I. AUTONOMOUS TECHNOLOGY INDUSTRY

Create competing technology ecosystems.

Companies can independently develop:

- Operating systems.
- Programming languages.
- Development tools.
- AI models.
- CPUs and GPUs.
- Networking equipment.
- Smartphones.
- Cloud platforms.
- Databases.
- Security software.
- Developer frameworks.

Technologies should have versions, compatibility, licensing, documentation, and adoption rates.

Companies can compete for market share.

Open-source projects can become major industry standards.

J. ENTERTAINMENT AND DIGITAL CULTURE

Create an independent entertainment ecosystem.

Include:

- Gaming studios.
- Online games.
- Music platforms.
- Streaming services.
- Digital art.
- Content creators.
- Virtual communities.
- Esports organizations.
- Digital events.

NPCs can create games, publish music, form communities, participate in tournaments, and develop creative careers.

Players can build entertainment companies and publish their own products.

K. DIGITAL IDENTITY AND REPUTATION

Create a unified identity system.

Each individual has:

- Personal accounts.
- Professional profiles.
- Public reputation.
- Private relationships.
- Digital credentials.
- Employment history.
- Published work.
- Financial identity.
- Security history.

Reputation must be contextual.

A person can be respected professionally but controversial in a social community.

A developer can become famous within a programming ecosystem without being famous to the general population.

L. DYNAMIC WORLD EVENTS

Introduce long-term emergent events.

Examples:

- A major technological revolution.
- A global financial recession.
- A telecommunications disruption.
- A new software standard.
- A corporate monopoly investigation.
- A major scientific discovery.
- A regional energy crisis.
- A new internet infrastructure project.
- A major cybersecurity incident.
- A global supply shortage.

Events should emerge from interconnected simulation systems.

They must create consequences that can persist for years of simulated time.

M. MULTIPLAYER AND SHARED CIVILIZATION

Design the architecture to support optional multiplayer.

Allow multiple human players to inhabit the same persistent world.

Players can:

- Start companies together.
- Employ each other.
- Trade assets.
- Develop software.
- Establish communities.
- Own infrastructure.
- Compete in markets.
- Build organizations.
- Negotiate contracts.

The world must remain functional if other players disconnect.

NPCs should continue filling the economic and social ecosystem.

Implement authoritative server-side financial transactions, permission controls, secure identity management, anti-cheat systems, and persistent shared world states.

N. LIVING HISTORICAL TIMELINE

Maintain a complete world history.

Record:

- New businesses.
- Scientific discoveries.
- Political decisions.
- Market crashes.
- Technological releases.
- Major NPC achievements.
- Wars and diplomatic events within the fictional world.
- Infrastructure development.
- Social movements.
- Cultural changes.

Allow players to explore historical timelines, discover past events, and investigate how the world reached its current state.

O. WORLD SIMULATION INTELLIGENCE

Create an interconnected simulation architecture with several levels.

1. Individual simulation: needs, personality, memory and decisions.
2. Household simulation: relationships, housing and shared finances.
3. Organization simulation: employees, management and business objectives.
4. City simulation: infrastructure, population and economic activity.
5. Country simulation: institutions, regulations and economic conditions.
6. Global simulation: trade, technology, finance and geopolitical relationships.
7. Internet simulation: networks, services, data and communication.

Changes at one level must propagate to relevant other levels.

Use efficient event-driven processing and abstraction.

Do not run expensive AI inference continuously for every NPC.

Use persistent state, specialized behavioral models, scheduled decision-making, and contextual AI generation.

P. FINAL DESIGN PHILOSOPHY

There must be no artificial requirement for the player to be successful.

The player may become:

- A programmer.
- A researcher.
- An investor.
- A business owner.
- A network engineer.
- A journalist.
- A digital entrepreneur.
- A software developer.
- An independent citizen.

The player may also remain an ordinary individual with a small computer and a few personal projects.

The world must remain interesting regardless of the player's wealth or reputation.

Build a civilization, not a sequence of missions.

Every system must contribute to the same persistent world.

The game should support years of simulated history without requiring a reset.

THE WORLD EXISTS BEFORE THE PLAYER, EVOLVES DURING THEIR ABSENCE, AND CONTINUES AFTER THEIR ACTIONS."

Include:

- Gaming studios.
- Online games.
- Music platforms.
- Streaming services.
- Digital art.
- Content creators.
- Virtual communities.
- Esports organizations.
- Digital events.

NPCs can create games, publish music, form communities, participate in tournaments, and develop creative careers.

Players can build entertainment companies and publish their own products.

K. DIGITAL IDENTITY AND REPUTATION

Create a unified identity system.

Each individual has:

- Personal accounts.
- Professional profiles.
- Public reputation.
- Private relationships.
- Digital credentials.
- Employment history.
- Published work.
- Financial identity.
- Security history.

Reputation must be contextual.

A person can be respected professionally but controversial in a social community.

A developer can become famous within a programming ecosystem without being famous to the general population.

L. DYNAMIC WORLD EVENTS

Introduce long-term emergent events.

Examples:

- A major technological revolution.
- A global financial recession.
- A telecommunications disruption.
- A new software standard.
- A corporate monopoly investigation.
- A major scientific discovery.
- A regional energy crisis.
- A new internet infrastructure project.
- A major cybersecurity incident.
- A global supply shortage.

Events should emerge from interconnected simulation systems.

They must create consequences that can persist for years of simulated time.

M. MULTIPLAYER AND SHARED CIVILIZATION

Design the architecture to support optional multiplayer.

Allow multiple human players to inhabit the same persistent world.

Players can:

- Start companies together.
- Employ each other.
- Trade assets.
- Develop software.
- Establish communities.
- Own infrastructure.
- Compete in markets.
- Build organizations.
- Negotiate contracts.

The world must remain functional if other players disconnect.

NPCs should continue filling the economic and social ecosystem.

Implement authoritative server-side financial transactions, permission controls, secure identity management, anti-cheat systems, and persistent shared world states.

N. LIVING HISTORICAL TIMELINE

Maintain a complete world history.

Record:

- New businesses.
- Scientific discoveries.
- Political decisions.
- Market crashes.
- Technological releases.
- Major NPC achievements.
- Wars and diplomatic events within the fictional world.
- Infrastructure development.
- Social movements.
- Cultural changes.

Allow players to explore historical timelines, discover past events, and investigate how the world reached its current state.

O. WORLD SIMULATION INTELLIGENCE

Create an interconnected simulation architecture with several levels.

1. Individual simulation: needs, personality, memory and decisions.
2. Household simulation: relationships, housing and shared finances.
3. Organization simulation: employees, management and business objectives.
4. City simulation: infrastructure, population and economic activity.
5. Country simulation: institutions, regulations and economic conditions.
6. Global simulation: trade, technology, finance and geopolitical relationships.
7. Internet simulation: networks, services, data and communication.

Changes at one level must propagate to relevant other levels.

Use efficient event-driven processing and abstraction.

Do not run expensive AI inference continuously for every NPC.

Use persistent state, specialized behavioral models, scheduled decision-making, and contextual AI generation.

P. FINAL DESIGN PHILOSOPHY

There must be no artificial requirement for the player to be successful.

The player may become:

- A programmer.
- A researcher.
- An investor.
- A business owner.
- A network engineer.
- A journalist.
- A digital entrepreneur.
- A software developer.
- An independent citizen.

The player may also remain an ordinary individual with a small computer and a few personal projects.

The world must remain interesting regardless of the player's wealth or reputation.

Build a civilization, not a sequence of missions.

Every system must contribute to the same persistent world.

The game should support years of simulated history without requiring a reset.

THE WORLD EXISTS BEFORE THE PLAYER, EVOLVES DURING THEIR ABSENCE, AND CONTINUES AFTER THEIR ACTIONS."

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Expand “INTERNET: PERSISTENT WORLD” into a persistent digital civilization simulation, while continuing the existing procedural growth work.

## Requirements
- Preserve existing features and shared persistent world, economy, NPC population, databases, and historical timeline.
- Simulate countries and regions with governments, institutions, economies, currencies, populations, internet infrastructure, providers, taxation, digital regulations, finance, universities, and technology industries.
- Model international relations, trade agreements, regulation, technological competition, sanctions, diplomacy, and cyber policy.
- Support independent play without requiring wealth, reputation, a career, or missions; the world should evolve during player absence and continue over years without resets.
- Avoid continuous expensive AI inference for every NPC; use persistent state, specialized behavior, scheduled decisions, and contextual AI generation.

## Decisions
- Use `tickWorld()` as the primary integration point for procedural growth.
- Apply bounded cadence helpers and restore missing growth metadata only in `reviveGame()`.
- Maintain entity caps: 30 companies, 420 NPCs, 180 servers, 220 sites, and 60 open contracts.
- Initialize `lastRentDay` from world time only when it is missing.

## Work State
### Completed
- Added growth metadata and restore logic for older saves, including `lastRentDay` compatibility.
- Added deterministic bounded growth for companies, NPCs, servers, sites, contracts, and news/events; integrated it into `tickWorld()`.
- Fixed the initial `TLDs` typo and added the `TLDS` form.
- Passed module syntax checks, save/revival serialization, a 5,000-world-minute smoke test, and `git diff --check`.

### Active
- Integrate the requested digital-civilization systems into the existing game without removing or simplifying prior features.
- Broaden validation to progression and save/reload across larger entity and offline simulation workloads.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect the current diff and codebase to identify integration points for the new civilization systems.
2. Run broader progression, save/reload, and offline simulation checks.
3. Confirm the final diff has no unintended changes and whitespace remains clean.

## Relevant Files
- `src/world.js`: Growth metadata, bounded cadence helpers, entity builders, revival, and `tickWorld()` integration.
- `src/data.js`: Company, contract, news, and site-generation templates.
- `src/systems.js`: Cloud, container, agent, organization, and auxiliary simulation.
- `src/main.js`: Persistence and offline simulation/reporting.
- `src/shell.js`: Terminal gameplay behavior.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted across `index.html`, `src/data.js`, `src/main.js`, `src/shell.js`, `src/world.js`, and `styles.css`; `src/systems.js` is untracked.
- `tickWorld()` seeds RNG from `game.seed`, `game.worldMinutes`, and `game.tickCount`; offline simulation advances it in bounded chunks.
- `generateContract()` depends on existing servers and NPCs; news and feed caps are 70 and 80 entries.
- Cloud rent is charged per crossed world day; owned-site revenue is processed at crossed 10-minute boundaries.
- The smoke test reached 21 companies, 119 NPCs, 198 servers, 88 sites, and 20 contracts after 5,000 minutes, with `game.lastRentDay = 3`.

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Expand “INTERNET: PERSISTENT WORLD” into a persistent digital civilization simulation that builds on the existing procedural growth work without removing prior features.

## Requirements
- Integrate geopolitics, law, education, research, media, physical infrastructure, property, supply chains, technology, entertainment, identity, emergent events, multiplayer architecture, historical timelines, and interconnected simulation layers into the same persistent world.
- Support independent play at any level of success; the world should evolve during player absence and continue for years without resets.
- Avoid continuous expensive AI inference for every NPC; use persistent state, specialized behavior, scheduled decisions, and contextual AI generation.

## Decisions
- Use `tickWorld()` as the primary integration point for procedural growth.
- Apply bounded cadence helpers and restore missing growth metadata only in `reviveGame()`.
- Maintain entity caps: 30 companies, 420 NPCs, 180 servers, 220 sites, and 60 open contracts.
- Initialize `lastRentDay` from world time only when it is missing.

## Work State
### Completed
- Added growth metadata and restore logic for older saves, including `lastRentDay` compatibility.
- Added deterministic bounded growth for companies, NPCs, servers, sites, contracts, and news/events; integrated it into `tickWorld()`.
- Fixed the initial `TLDs` typo and added the `TLDS` form.
- Passed module syntax checks, save/revival serialization, a 5,000-world-minute smoke test, and `git diff --check`.

### Active
- Integrate the requested digital-civilization systems into the existing game without removing or simplifying prior features.
- Broaden validation to progression and save/reload across larger entity and offline simulation workloads.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect the current diff and codebase to identify integration points for the new civilization systems.
2. Run broader progression, save/reload, and offline simulation checks.
3. Confirm the final diff has no unintended changes and whitespace remains clean.

## Relevant Files
- `src/world.js`: Growth metadata, bounded cadence helpers, entity builders, revival, and `tickWorld()` integration.
- `src/data.js`: Company, contract, news, and site-generation templates.
- `src/systems.js`: Cloud, container, agent, organization, and auxiliary simulation.
- `src/main.js`: Persistence and offline simulation/reporting.
- `src/shell.js`: Terminal gameplay behavior.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted across `index.html`, `src/data.js`, `src/main.js`, `src/shell.js`, `src/world.js`, and `styles.css`; `src/systems.js` is untracked.
- `tickWorld()` seeds RNG from `game.seed`, `game.worldMinutes`, and `game.tickCount`; offline simulation advances it in bounded chunks.
- `generateContract()` depends on existing servers and NPCs; news and feed caps are 70 and 80 entries.
- Cloud rent is charged per crossed world day; owned-site revenue is processed at crossed 10-minute boundaries.
- The smoke test reached 21 companies, 119 NPCs, 198 servers, 88 sites, and 20 contracts after 5,000 minutes, with `game.lastRentDay = 3`.

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Expand “INTERNET: PERSISTENT WORLD” into a persistent digital civilization simulation that builds on existing procedural growth without removing prior features.

## Requirements
- Integrate geopolitics, law, education, research, media, infrastructure, property, supply chains, technology, entertainment, identity, emergent events, multiplayer architecture, historical timelines, and interconnected simulation layers.
- Allow play at any success level; evolve the world during player absence and support years of persistence without resets.
- Avoid continuous expensive AI inference for every NPC; use persistent state, specialized behavior, scheduled decisions, and contextual AI generation.

## Decisions
- Use `tickWorld()` as the primary integration point for procedural growth.
- Apply bounded cadence helpers and restore missing growth metadata only in `reviveGame()`.
- Maintain caps: 30 companies, 420 NPCs, 180 servers, 220 sites, and 60 open contracts.
- Initialize `lastRentDay` from world time only when missing.

## Work State
### Completed
- Added deterministic, bounded growth for companies, NPCs, servers, sites, contracts, news, and events, integrated into `tickWorld()`.
- Added growth metadata and compatibility restoration for older saves, including `lastRentDay`.
- Added civilization simulation and interfaces: `src/civilization.js` is imported by `src/world.js`, `src/main.js`, and `src/shell.js`; shell supports `civ` commands for civilization systems.
- Fixed the initial `TLDs` typo and added the `TLDS` form.
- Passed module syntax checks, save/revival serialization, a 5,000-world-minute smoke test, and `git diff --check`.

### Active
- Review the full current diff and validate civilization-system progression, save/reload, and larger offline-simulation workloads.
- Confirm the implementation preserves existing features and has no unintended changes.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect the current diff and civilization integration in `src/civilization.js`, `src/world.js`, `src/main.js`, and `src/shell.js`.
2. Run broader progression, save/reload, and offline simulation checks.
3. Review the final diff and verify whitespace cleanliness.

## Relevant Files
- `src/civilization.js`: Civilization simulation and interfaces for law, education, research, media, property, supply, history, and multiplayer.
- `src/world.js`: Growth metadata, bounded cadence helpers, revival, and `tickWorld()` integration.
- `src/systems.js`: Cloud, container, agent, organization, and auxiliary simulation; untracked.
- `src/main.js`: Persistence, offline simulation/reporting, and civilization UI integration.
- `src/shell.js`: Terminal gameplay behavior and civilization commands.
- `src/data.js`: Generation templates and simulation data.
- `index.html`: UI structure changes.
- `styles.css`: UI styling changes.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted across `index.html`, `src/data.js`, `src/main.js`, `src/shell.js`, `src/world.js`, and `styles.css`; `src/systems.js` is untracked.
- `tickWorld()` seeds RNG from `game.seed`, `game.worldMinutes`, and `game.tickCount`; offline simulation advances in bounded chunks.
- `generateContract()` depends on existing servers and NPCs; news and feed caps are 70 and 80 entries.
- Cloud rent is charged per crossed world day; owned-site revenue is processed at crossed 10-minute boundaries.
- The 5,000-minute smoke test reached 21 companies, 119 NPCs, 198 servers, 88 sites, and 20 contracts; `game.lastRentDay = 3`.

INTERNET: PERSISTENT WORLD

ULTIMATE WORLD EXPANSION — GLOBAL DIGITAL CIVILIZATION


CORE DIRECTIVE


Expand every aspect of the existing game into a deeply interconnected, persistent, autonomous digital civilization.


Do not limit development to hacking, programming, networking, or financial markets.


The player must inhabit an entire simulated digital society containing millions of potential interactions, evolving institutions, technologies, communities, economies, businesses, individuals, and interconnected systems.


The internet must exist independently of the player.


The world must continue developing, changing, competing, innovating, experiencing crises, and creating opportunities whether the player is online or offline.


Preserve every existing working system. Expand the existing architecture rather than replacing it.


---


1. GLOBAL DIGITAL GEOGRAPHY


Create a detailed global world divided into:


- Countries and territories.
- Cities and metropolitan regions.
- Technology districts.
- Industrial zones.
- University districts.
- Financial centers.
- Residential areas.
- Data center regions.
- Telecommunications hubs.
- Research campuses.
- Startup ecosystems.
- Internet exchange locations.


Each region has its own technological development, economic conditions, infrastructure quality, regulations, labor market, culture, and cost of living.


Geography must influence network latency, hosting costs, business opportunities, employment, and infrastructure availability.


2. COMPLETE HUMAN SOCIETY


Expand NPC simulation into a complete social civilization.


Every individual should have:


- A unique identity.
- Age and life history.
- Education and qualifications.
- Technical abilities.
- Personality and behavioral tendencies.
- Financial situation.
- Employment history.
- Family and friendships.
- Professional relationships.
- Personal interests.
- Long-term ambitions.
- Daily routines.
- Memories and experiences.
- Opinions and preferences.
- Personal online identity.


NPCs should independently make decisions.


They can study, change careers, move cities, establish businesses, become unemployed, develop friendships, create communities, retire, and influence society.


Introduce households, families, social circles, professional networks, and generational changes.


Avoid making every NPC interact with the player.


3. EDUCATION AND KNOWLEDGE ECONOMY


Create an extensive education system.


Include:


- Universities.
- Technical colleges.
- Online academies.
- Independent researchers.
- Professional certifications.
- Programming courses.
- Network engineering education.
- Business administration.
- Economics.
- Mathematics.
- Artificial intelligence.
- Cybersecurity.
- Scientific research.


Players can acquire knowledge through documentation, courses, experimentation, projects, and professional experience.


NPCs should develop expertise over time.


New discoveries and research publications can influence technology, companies, markets, and society.


4. COMPLETE BUSINESS AND CORPORATE ECOSYSTEM


Create a highly detailed corporate world.


Organizations should include:


- Small independent businesses.
- Freelance agencies.
- Software studios.
- Hosting companies.
- Cloud providers.
- Telecommunications operators.
- AI companies.
- Hardware manufacturers.
- Financial technology companies.
- Cybersecurity firms.
- Media organizations.
- Online marketplaces.
- Research companies.
- Global technology corporations.


Every organization should have internal operations:


- Executives.
- Departments.
- Employees.
- Recruitment.
- Payroll.
- Accounting.
- Taxes.
- Budgets.
- Contracts.
- Customers.
- Suppliers.
- Assets.
- Debts.
- Investments.
- Products.
- Research.
- Marketing.
- Customer support.


Companies can compete, collaborate, acquire competitors, merge, expand internationally, restructure, and go bankrupt.


Introduce realistic organizational hierarchies and corporate politics.


5. HARDWARE AND TECHNOLOGY INDUSTRY


Create an evolving hardware ecosystem.


Include:


- CPUs.
- GPUs.
- RAM.
- Motherboards.
- Storage devices.
- Servers.
- Workstations.
- Laptops.
- Smartphones.
- Routers.
- Switches.
- Network appliances.
- Fiber infrastructure.
- Data center equipment.
- Cooling systems.
- Power infrastructure.


Components have specifications, prices, performance characteristics, compatibility requirements, reliability, and lifespans.


Manufacturers research and release new generations of hardware.


Players can build custom computers, purchase equipment, establish server rooms, operate data centers, and develop hardware businesses.


Supply shortages, manufacturing disruptions, technological advances, and component prices must affect the economy.


6. SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGICAL PROGRESSION


Introduce a global research and innovation system.


Technologies should evolve through:


- Research.
- Development.
- Testing.
- Prototypes.
- Commercialization.
- Adoption.
- Standardization.
- Obsolescence.


Include emerging fields such as:


- Quantum computing.
- Advanced AI.
- Robotics.
- Distributed computing.
- Advanced cryptography.
- Satellite internet.
- Biotechnology information systems.
- Autonomous infrastructure.
- New programming paradigms.


NPC researchers and organizations independently contribute to technological progress.


The player can participate in research or build companies around new discoveries.


7. MEDIA, ENTERTAINMENT AND DIGITAL CULTURE


Create a thriving digital entertainment ecosystem.


Include:


- Video platforms.
- Streaming services.
- Music platforms.
- Digital publishing.
- Gaming communities.
- Online influencers.
- Independent creators.
- News organizations.
- Podcasts.
- Digital magazines.
- Online events.
- Esports organizations.
- Virtual communities.


Content creators should have audiences, reputations, revenue, subscribers, competitors, and changing popularity.


Trends emerge organically and spread through social networks.


Players can create channels, publish software tutorials, build audiences, produce entertainment, and establish media companies.


8. INTERNET CULTURE AND COMMUNITIES


Generate thousands of distinct digital communities.


Examples:


- Programming communities.
- Linux communities.
- Gaming forums.
- Cryptocurrency communities.
- Academic networks.
- Hardware enthusiasts.
- Independent developers.
- Digital artists.
- Entrepreneurs.
- Technology journalists.
- Security researchers.


Communities develop their own rules, moderators, reputations, traditions, conflicts, and histories.


NPCs create discussions, publish tutorials, answer questions, organize events, and form partnerships.


Community reputation should influence professional opportunities.


9. POLITICS, LAW AND INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS


Introduce a realistic institutional environment.


Include:


- Governments.
- Digital regulatory agencies.
- Courts.
- Tax authorities.
- Consumer protection agencies.
- Data protection regulators.
- Telecommunications regulators.
- International standards organizations.


Countries have different laws, tax systems, internet policies, economic conditions, and technology strategies.


Regulations can affect hosting, data storage, software distribution, cybersecurity, financial services, and international business.


Introduce international cooperation, trade agreements, digital disputes, regulatory changes, and geopolitical events.


10. PERSONAL LIFE AND DIGITAL LIFESTYLE


Expand the player's everyday existence.


The player should manage:


- Personal finances.
- Housing.
- Computer equipment.
- Internet subscriptions.
- Electricity costs.
- Software subscriptions.
- Personal accounts.
- Professional reputation.
- Contacts.
- Email.
- Work schedules.
- Business commitments.
- Learning goals.


Allow the player to begin with limited resources and gradually develop a professional digital life.


Introduce realistic expenses, income sources, financial obligations, and lifestyle upgrades.


11. EMPLOYMENT AND PROFESSIONAL CAREERS


Create a dynamic global job market.


NPC companies publish job offers.


Players can apply, submit resumes, complete interviews, negotiate salaries, accept contracts, work remotely, freelance, or establish independent businesses.


Careers include:


- Software developer.
- Network engineer.
- Systems administrator.
- Cloud architect.
- AI engineer.
- Security analyst.
- Research scientist.
- IT technician.
- Technical consultant.
- Business owner.
- Digital marketer.
- Data analyst.
- Journalist.
- Content creator.


Professional skills should develop through actual work and experience.


Employers evaluate experience, qualifications, reputation, and demonstrated abilities.


12. TRANSPORTATION AND PHYSICAL INFRASTRUCTURE


Represent the physical world supporting the digital civilization.


Include:


- Electricity grids.
- Power plants.
- Renewable energy.
- Roads.
- Railways.
- Ports.
- Airports.
- Industrial facilities.
- Data center cooling.
- Cable landing stations.
- Satellite ground stations.


Physical disruptions should influence digital services.


Power failures can affect data centers. Construction can improve connectivity. Natural disasters can damage infrastructure.


13. DYNAMIC WORLD EVENTS


Create a persistent global event engine.


Generate events at multiple scales:


LOCAL:


- A startup opens.
- A local ISP changes its plans.
- A developer community organizes an event.
- A server becomes unavailable.


REGIONAL:


- A data center expands.
- A university launches a research program.
- A regional network experiences congestion.
- A technology company recruits hundreds of employees.


GLOBAL:


- A new computing architecture emerges.
- A major technology corporation changes strategy.
- An international cyber incident occurs.
- A global supply shortage affects hardware.
- A new internet standard becomes widely adopted.
- An economic recession affects technology investment.


Events must have causes, consequences, affected entities, and historical records.


14. COMPLEX EMERGENT ECONOMY


Expand the economic simulation into a complete interconnected system.


Include:


- Employment markets.
- Housing markets.
- Hardware markets.
- Software markets.
- Hosting markets.
- Cloud computing markets.
- Advertising markets.
- Subscription services.
- Freelance marketplaces.
- Intellectual property.
- Business acquisitions.
- Venture capital.
- Loans.
- Insurance.
- Taxes.
- International trade.


Prices must respond to supply, demand, competition, production costs, innovation, and economic conditions.


Introduce inflation, interest rates, unemployment, recessions, growth cycles, and financial crises.


All financial activity must remain simulated and use fictional in-game assets.


15. PERSONAL PROJECT ECOSYSTEM


Allow players to maintain multiple projects simultaneously.


Examples:


- A personal website.
- A software application.
- A game studio.
- A hosting business.
- A social network.
- An AI service.
- A research project.
- A marketplace.
- A private server network.
- An online publication.


Projects have development stages, resources, expenses, dependencies, users, maintenance requirements, and potential revenue.


NPCs can discover, use, review, contribute to, compete with, or purchase player projects.


16. WORLD HISTORY AND LEGACY


Create a permanent historical record of civilization.


Record:


- Founding of companies.
- Technological discoveries.
- Network expansions.
- Major software releases.
- Business failures.
- Economic crises.
- Important NPC lives.
- Community movements.
- Major infrastructure projects.
- Political decisions.
- Player achievements.


Allow players to explore historical timelines and understand how the world evolved.


A company founded by an NPC years ago should have a history that can be investigated.


The world should develop recognizable historical eras.


17. DEEP SIMULATION ARCHITECTURE


Implement a unified simulation framework.


All systems must share consistent data and influence one another.


Examples:


- A new GPU architecture reduces AI hosting costs.
- Lower hosting costs allow new AI startups to emerge.
- New startups recruit developers.
- Increased hiring changes salaries.
- New services attract users.
- Increased traffic creates network demand.
- Network demand encourages infrastructure investment.
- Infrastructure investment creates new jobs.


This interconnected causality is essential.


Use:


- Hierarchical simulation.
- Event-driven architecture.
- Deterministic simulation where appropriate.
- Persistent entity identifiers.
- Efficient NPC abstraction.
- Regional simulation.
- Background progression.
- Historical event logs.
- Incremental saving.
- Recoverable world states.


Avoid expensive continuous simulation of irrelevant entities.


18. USER INTERFACE EXPANSION


Preserve the realistic Linux workstation aesthetic.


The main interface should remain centered around the terminal.


Add optional integrated applications:


- File manager.
- Web browser.
- Network monitor.
- System monitor.
- Code editor.
- Email client.
- Messaging client.
- Market terminal.
- Company management.
- Cloud dashboard.
- Server administration.
- Social platform.
- World map.
- Research database.


Applications should represent actual simulation systems, not decorative menus.


Maintain an intuitive mobile interface suitable for Android screens.


19. DEVELOPMENT RULES


This is an expansion of the existing game, not a replacement.


Strictly preserve:


- Existing working terminal commands.
- Existing save data compatibility.
- Existing player identity.
- Existing economic systems.
- Existing NPCs.
- Existing companies.
- Existing market history.
- Existing world state.


Use versioned save migrations when new systems require additional data.


All new systems must integrate with existing entity IDs and shared simulation state.


Avoid creating disconnected features that do not interact with the world.


Prioritize functional mechanics over decorative interfaces.


Do not claim a system is implemented until it is actually playable and tested.


FINAL VISION


Create a complete digital civilization simulator where technology, economics, human society, business, science, politics, culture, infrastructure, and personal life evolve together.


The player should be able to spend hundreds of hours building a life inside this world without exhausting its possibilities.


They might become a programmer, researcher, entrepreneur, corporate executive, network engineer, investor, creator, or simply an ordinary internet user.


The world must not exist to serve the player.


The player exists inside the world.


INTERNET: PERSISTENT WORLD — A LIVING DIGITAL CIVILIZATION, NOT JUST A GAME ABOUT COMPUTERS.

- Background progression.

- Incremental saving.
- Recoverable world states.

- Web browser.
- Network monitor.
- System monitor.
- Code editor.
- Email client.
- Messaging client.
- Market terminal.
- Company management.
- Cloud dashboard.
- Server administration.
- Social platform.
- World map.
- Research database.


Applications should represent actual simulation systems, not decorative menus.


Maintain an intuitive mobile interface suitable for Android screens.

This is an expansion of the existing game, not a replacement.


Strictly preserve:


- Existing working terminal commands.
- Existing save data compatibility.
- Existing player identity.
- Existing economic systems.
- Existing NPCs.
- Existing companies.
- Existing market history.
- Existing world state.

All new systems must integrate with existing entity IDs and shared simulation state.


Avoid creating disconnected features that do not interact with the world.


Prioritize functional mechanics over decorative interfaces.


Do not claim a system is implemented until it is actually playable and tested.

The world must not exist to serve the player.


The player exists inside the world.

"INTERNET: PERSISTENT WORLD

ULTIMATE WORLD EXPANSION — GLOBAL DIGITAL CIVILIZATION

CORE DIRECTIVE

Expand every aspect of the existing game into a deeply interconnected, persistent, autonomous digital civilization.

Do not limit development to hacking, programming, networking, or financial markets.

The player must inhabit an entire simulated digital society containing millions of potential interactions, evolving institutions, technologies, communities, economies, businesses, individuals, and interconnected systems.

The internet must exist independently of the player.

The world must continue developing, changing, competing, innovating, experiencing crises, and creating opportunities whether the player is online or offline.

Preserve every existing working system. Expand the existing architecture rather than replacing it.

---

1. GLOBAL DIGITAL GEOGRAPHY

Create a detailed global world divided into:

- Countries and territories.
- Cities and metropolitan regions.
- Technology districts.
- Industrial zones.
- University districts.
- Financial centers.
- Residential areas.
- Data center regions.
- Telecommunications hubs.
- Research campuses.
- Startup ecosystems.
- Internet exchange locations.

Each region has its own technological development, economic conditions, infrastructure quality, regulations, labor market, culture, and cost of living.

Geography must influence network latency, hosting costs, business opportunities, employment, and infrastructure availability.

2. COMPLETE HUMAN SOCIETY

Expand NPC simulation into a complete social civilization.

Every individual should have:

- A unique identity.
- Age and life history.
- Education and qualifications.
- Technical abilities.
- Personality and behavioral tendencies.
- Financial situation.
- Employment history.
- Family and friendships.
- Professional relationships.
- Personal interests.
- Long-term ambitions.
- Daily routines.
- Memories and experiences.
- Opinions and preferences.
- Personal online identity.

NPCs should independently make decisions.

They can study, change careers, move cities, establish businesses, become unemployed, develop friendships, create communities, retire, and influence society.

Introduce households, families, social circles, professional networks, and generational changes.

Avoid making every NPC interact with the player.

3. EDUCATION AND KNOWLEDGE ECONOMY

Create an extensive education system.

Include:

- Universities.
- Technical colleges.
- Online academies.
- Independent researchers.
- Professional certifications.
- Programming courses.
- Network engineering education.
- Business administration.
- Economics.
- Mathematics.
- Artificial intelligence.
- Cybersecurity.
- Scientific research.

Players can acquire knowledge through documentation, courses, experimentation, projects, and professional experience.

NPCs should develop expertise over time.

New discoveries and research publications can influence technology, companies, markets, and society.

4. COMPLETE BUSINESS AND CORPORATE ECOSYSTEM

Create a highly detailed corporate world.

Organizations should include:

- Small independent businesses.
- Freelance agencies.
- Software studios.
- Hosting companies.
- Cloud providers.
- Telecommunications operators.
- AI companies.
- Hardware manufacturers.
- Financial technology companies.
- Cybersecurity firms.
- Media organizations.
- Online marketplaces.
- Research companies.
- Global technology corporations.

Every organization should have internal operations:

- Executives.
- Departments.
- Employees.
- Recruitment.
- Payroll.
- Accounting.
- Taxes.
- Budgets.
- Contracts.
- Customers.
- Suppliers.
- Assets.
- Debts.
- Investments.
- Products.
- Research.
- Marketing.
- Customer support.

Companies can compete, collaborate, acquire competitors, merge, expand internationally, restructure, and go bankrupt.

Introduce realistic organizational hierarchies and corporate politics.

5. HARDWARE AND TECHNOLOGY INDUSTRY

Create an evolving hardware ecosystem.

Include:

- CPUs.
- GPUs.
- RAM.
- Motherboards.
- Storage devices.
- Servers.
- Workstations.
- Laptops.
- Smartphones.
- Routers.
- Switches.
- Network appliances.
- Fiber infrastructure.
- Data center equipment.
- Cooling systems.
- Power infrastructure.

Components have specifications, prices, performance characteristics, compatibility requirements, reliability, and lifespans.

Manufacturers research and release new generations of hardware.

Players can build custom computers, purchase equipment, establish server rooms, operate data centers, and develop hardware businesses.

Supply shortages, manufacturing disruptions, technological advances, and component prices must affect the economy.

6. SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGICAL PROGRESSION

Introduce a global research and innovation system.

Technologies should evolve through:

- Research.
- Development.
- Testing.
- Prototypes.
- Commercialization.
- Adoption.
- Standardization.
- Obsolescence.

Include emerging fields such as:

- Quantum computing.
- Advanced AI.
- Robotics.
- Distributed computing.
- Advanced cryptography.
- Satellite internet.
- Biotechnology information systems.
- Autonomous infrastructure.
- New programming paradigms.

NPC researchers and organizations independently contribute to technological progress.

The player can participate in research or build companies around new discoveries.

7. MEDIA, ENTERTAINMENT AND DIGITAL CULTURE

Create a thriving digital entertainment ecosystem.

Include:

- Video platforms.
- Streaming services.
- Music platforms.
- Digital publishing.
- Gaming communities.
- Online influencers.
- Independent creators.
- News organizations.
- Podcasts.
- Digital magazines.
- Online events.
- Esports organizations.
- Virtual communities.

Content creators should have audiences, reputations, revenue, subscribers, competitors, and changing popularity.

Trends emerge organically and spread through social networks.

Players can create channels, publish software tutorials, build audiences, produce entertainment, and establish media companies.

8. INTERNET CULTURE AND COMMUNITIES

Generate thousands of distinct digital communities.

Examples:

- Programming communities.
- Linux communities.
- Gaming forums.
- Cryptocurrency communities.
- Academic networks.
- Hardware enthusiasts.
- Independent developers.
- Digital artists.
- Entrepreneurs.
- Technology journalists.
- Security researchers.

Communities develop their own rules, moderators, reputations, traditions, conflicts, and histories.

NPCs create discussions, publish tutorials, answer questions, organize events, and form partnerships.

Community reputation should influence professional opportunities.

9. POLITICS, LAW AND INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS

Introduce a realistic institutional environment.

Include:

- Governments.
- Digital regulatory agencies.
- Courts.
- Tax authorities.
- Consumer protection agencies.
- Data protection regulators.
- Telecommunications regulators.
- International standards organizations.

Countries have different laws, tax systems, internet policies, economic conditions, and technology strategies.

Regulations can affect hosting, data storage, software distribution, cybersecurity, financial services, and international business.

Introduce international cooperation, trade agreements, digital disputes, regulatory changes, and geopolitical events.

10. PERSONAL LIFE AND DIGITAL LIFESTYLE

Expand the player's everyday existence.

The player should manage:

- Personal finances.
- Housing.
- Computer equipment.
- Internet subscriptions.
- Electricity costs.
- Software subscriptions.
- Personal accounts.
- Professional reputation.
- Contacts.
- Email.
- Work schedules.
- Business commitments.
- Learning goals.

Allow the player to begin with limited resources and gradually develop a professional digital life.

Introduce realistic expenses, income sources, financial obligations, and lifestyle upgrades.

11. EMPLOYMENT AND PROFESSIONAL CAREERS

Create a dynamic global job market.

NPC companies publish job offers.

Players can apply, submit resumes, complete interviews, negotiate salaries, accept contracts, work remotely, freelance, or establish independent businesses.

Careers include:

- Software developer.
- Network engineer.
- Systems administrator.
- Cloud architect.
- AI engineer.
- Security analyst.
- Research scientist.
- IT technician.
- Technical consultant.
- Business owner.
- Digital marketer.
- Data analyst.
- Journalist.
- Content creator.

Professional skills should develop through actual work and experience.

Employers evaluate experience, qualifications, reputation, and demonstrated abilities.

12. TRANSPORTATION AND PHYSICAL INFRASTRUCTURE

Represent the physical world supporting the digital civilization.

Include:

- Electricity grids.
- Power plants.
- Renewable energy.
- Roads.
- Railways.
- Ports.
- Airports.
- Industrial facilities.
- Data center cooling.
- Cable landing stations.
- Satellite ground stations.

Physical disruptions should influence digital services.

Power failures can affect data centers. Construction can improve connectivity. Natural disasters can damage infrastructure.

13. DYNAMIC WORLD EVENTS

Create a persistent global event engine.

Generate events at multiple scales:

LOCAL:

- A startup opens.
- A local ISP changes its plans.
- A developer community organizes an event.
- A server becomes unavailable.

REGIONAL:

- A data center expands.
- A university launches a research program.
- A regional network experiences congestion.
- A technology company recruits hundreds of employees.

GLOBAL:

- A new computing architecture emerges.
- A major technology corporation changes strategy.
- An international cyber incident occurs.
- A global supply shortage affects hardware.
- A new internet standard becomes widely adopted.
- An economic recession affects technology investment.

Events must have causes, consequences, affected entities, and historical records.

14. COMPLEX EMERGENT ECONOMY

Expand the economic simulation into a complete interconnected system.

Include:

- Employment markets.
- Housing markets.
- Hardware markets.
- Software markets.
- Hosting markets.
- Cloud computing markets.
- Advertising markets.
- Subscription services.
- Freelance marketplaces.
- Intellectual property.
- Business acquisitions.
- Venture capital.
- Loans.
- Insurance.
- Taxes.
- International trade.

Prices must respond to supply, demand, competition, production costs, innovation, and economic conditions.

Introduce inflation, interest rates, unemployment, recessions, growth cycles, and financial crises.

All financial activity must remain simulated and use fictional in-game assets.

15. PERSONAL PROJECT ECOSYSTEM

Allow players to maintain multiple projects simultaneously.

Examples:

- A personal website.
- A software application.
- A game studio.
- A hosting business.
- A social network.
- An AI service.
- A research project.
- A marketplace.
- A private server network.
- An online publication.

Projects have development stages, resources, expenses, dependencies, users, maintenance requirements, and potential revenue.

NPCs can discover, use, review, contribute to, compete with, or purchase player projects.

16. WORLD HISTORY AND LEGACY

Create a permanent historical record of civilization.

Record:

- Founding of companies.
- Technological discoveries.
- Network expansions.
- Major software releases.
- Business failures.
- Economic crises.
- Important NPC lives.
- Community movements.
- Major infrastructure projects.
- Political decisions.
- Player achievements.

Allow players to explore historical timelines and understand how the world evolved.

A company founded by an NPC years ago should have a history that can be investigated.

The world should develop recognizable historical eras.

17. DEEP SIMULATION ARCHITECTURE

Implement a unified simulation framework.

All systems must share consistent data and influence one another.

Examples:

- A new GPU architecture reduces AI hosting costs.
- Lower hosting costs allow new AI startups to emerge.
- New startups recruit developers.
- Increased hiring changes salaries.
- New services attract users.
- Increased traffic creates network demand.
- Network demand encourages infrastructure investment.
- Infrastructure investment creates new jobs.

This interconnected causality is essential.

Use:

- Hierarchical simulation.
- Event-driven architecture.
- Deterministic simulation where appropriate.
- Persistent entity identifiers.
- Efficient NPC abstraction.
- Regional simulation.
- Background progression.
- Historical event logs.
- Incremental saving.
- Recoverable world states.

Avoid expensive continuous simulation of irrelevant entities.

18. USER INTERFACE EXPANSION

Preserve the realistic Linux workstation aesthetic.

The main interface should remain centered around the terminal.

Add optional integrated applications:

- File manager.
- Web browser.
- Network monitor.
- System monitor.
- Code editor.
- Email client.
- Messaging client.
- Market terminal.
- Company management.
- Cloud dashboard.
- Server administration.
- Social platform.
- World map.
- Research database.

Applications should represent actual simulation systems, not decorative menus.

Maintain an intuitive mobile interface suitable for Android screens.

19. DEVELOPMENT RULES

This is an expansion of the existing game, not a replacement.

Strictly preserve:

- Existing working terminal commands.
- Existing save data compatibility.
- Existing player identity.
- Existing economic systems.
- Existing NPCs.
- Existing companies.
- Existing market history.
- Existing world state.

Use versioned save migrations when new systems require additional data.

All new systems must integrate with existing entity IDs and shared simulation state.

Avoid creating disconnected features that do not interact with the world.

Prioritize functional mechanics over decorative interfaces.

Do not claim a system is implemented until it is actually playable and tested.

FINAL VISION

Create a complete digital civilization simulator where technology, economics, human society, business, science, politics, culture, infrastructure, and personal life evolve together.

The player should be able to spend hundreds of hours building a life inside this world without exhausting its possibilities.

They might become a programmer, researcher, entrepreneur, corporate executive, network engineer, investor, creator, or simply an ordinary internet user.

The world must not exist to serve the player.

The player exists inside the world.

INTERNET: PERSISTENT WORLD — A LIVING DIGITAL CIVILIZATION, NOT JUST A GAME ABOUT COMPUTERS."

Include:

- Universities.
- Technical colleges.
- Online academies.
- Independent researchers.
- Professional certifications.
- Programming courses.
- Network engineering education.
- Business administration.
- Economics.
- Mathematics.
- Artificial intelligence.
- Cybersecurity.
- Scientific research.

Players can acquire knowledge through documentation, courses, experimentation, projects, and professional experience.

NPCs should develop expertise over time.

New discoveries and research publications can influence technology, companies, markets, and society.

Create a highly detailed corporate world.

Organizations should include:

- Small independent businesses.
- Freelance agencies.
- Software studios.
- Hosting companies.
- Cloud providers.
- Telecommunications operators.
- AI companies.
- Hardware manufacturers.
- Financial technology companies.
- Cybersecurity firms.
- Media organizations.
- Online marketplaces.
- Research companies.
- Global technology corporations.

Every organization should have internal operations:

- Executives.
- Departments.
- Employees.
- Recruitment.
- Payroll.
- Accounting.
- Taxes.
- Budgets.
- Contracts.
- Customers.
- Suppliers.
- Assets.
- Debts.
- Investments.
- Products.
- Research.
- Marketing.
- Customer support.

Companies can compete, collaborate, acquire competitors, merge, expand internationally, restructure, and go bankrupt.

Introduce realistic organizational hierarchies and corporate politics.

5. HARDWARE AND TECHNOLOGY INDUSTRY

Create an evolving hardware ecosystem.

Include:

- CPUs.
- GPUs.
- RAM.
- Motherboards.
- Storage devices.
- Servers.
- Workstations.
- Laptops.
- Smartphones.
- Routers.
- Switches.
- Network appliances.
- Fiber infrastructure.
- Data center equipment.
- Cooling systems.
- Power infrastructure.

Components have specifications, prices, performance characteristics, compatibility requirements, reliability, and lifespans.

Manufacturers research and release new generations of hardware.

Players can build custom computers, purchase equipment, establish server rooms, operate data centers, and develop hardware businesses.

Supply shortages, manufacturing disruptions, technological advances, and component prices must affect the economy.

6. SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGICAL PROGRESSION

Introduce a global research and innovation system.

Technologies should evolve through:

- Research.
- Development.
- Testing.
- Prototypes.
- Commercialization.
- Adoption.
- Standardization.
- Obsolescence.

Include emerging fields such as:

- Quantum computing.
- Advanced AI.
- Robotics.
- Distributed computing.
- Advanced cryptography.
- Satellite internet.
- Biotechnology information systems.
- Autonomous infrastructure.
- New programming paradigms.

NPC researchers and organizations independently contribute to technological progress.

The player can participate in research or build companies around new discoveries.

7. MEDIA, ENTERTAINMENT AND DIGITAL CULTURE

Create a thriving digital entertainment ecosystem.

Include:

- Video platforms.
- Streaming services.
- Music platforms.
- Digital publishing.
- Gaming communities.
- Online influencers.
- Independent creators.
- News organizations.
- Podcasts.
- Digital magazines.
- Online events.
- Esports organizations.
- Virtual communities.

Content creators should have audiences, reputations, revenue, subscribers, competitors, and changing popularity.

Trends emerge organically and spread through social networks.

Players can create channels, publish software tutorials, build audiences, produce entertainment, and establish media companies.

8. INTERNET CULTURE AND COMMUNITIES

Generate thousands of distinct digital communities.

Examples:

- Programming communities.
- Linux communities.
- Gaming forums.
- Cryptocurrency communities.
- Academic networks.
- Hardware enthusiasts.
- Independent developers.
- Digital artists.
- Entrepreneurs.
- Technology journalists.
- Security researchers.

Communities develop their own rules, moderators, reputations, traditions, conflicts, and histories.

NPCs create discussions, publish tutorials, answer questions, organize events, and form partnerships.

Community reputation should influence professional opportunities.

9. POLITICS, LAW AND INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS

Introduce a realistic institutional environment.

Include:

- Governments.
- Digital regulatory agencies.
- Courts.
- Tax authorities.
- Consumer protection agencies.
- Data protection regulators.
- Telecommunications regulators.
- International standards organizations.

Countries have different laws, tax systems, internet policies, economic conditions, and technology strategies.

Regulations can affect hosting, data storage, software distribution, cybersecurity, financial services, and international business.

Introduce international cooperation, trade agreements, digital disputes, regulatory changes, and geopolitical events.

Expand the player's everyday existence.

- Personal finances.
- Housing.
- Computer equipment.
- Internet subscriptions.
- Electricity costs.
- Software subscriptions.
- Personal accounts.
- Professional reputation.
- Contacts.
- Email.
- Work schedules.
- Business commitments.
- Learning goals.

Introduce realistic expenses, income sources, financial obligations, and lifestyle upgrades.

Create a dynamic global job market.

NPC companies publish job offers.

Players can apply, submit resumes, complete interviews, negotiate salaries, accept contracts, work remotely, freelance, or establish independent businesses.

- Software developer.
- Network engineer.
- Systems administrator.
- Cloud architect.
- AI engineer.
- Security analyst.
- Research scientist.
- IT technician.
- Technical consultant.
- Business owner.
- Digital marketer.
- Data analyst.
- Journalist.
- Content creator.

Professional skills should develop through actual work and experience.

Employers evaluate experience, qualifications, reputation, and demonstrated abilities.

12. TRANSPORTATION AND PHYSICAL INFRASTRUCTURE

Represent the physical world supporting the digital civilization.

Include:

- Electricity grids.
- Power plants.
- Renewable energy.
- Roads.
- Railways.
- Ports.
- Airports.
- Industrial facilities.
- Data center cooling.
- Cable landing stations.
- Satellite ground stations.

Physical disruptions should influence digital services.

Power failures can affect data centers. Construction can improve connectivity. Natural disasters can damage infrastructure.

13. DYNAMIC WORLD EVENTS

Create a persistent global event engine.

Generate events at multiple scales:

LOCAL:

- A startup opens.
- A local ISP changes its plans.
- A developer community organizes an event.
- A server becomes unavailable.

REGIONAL:

- A data center expands.
- A university launches a research program.
- A regional network experiences congestion.
- A technology company recruits hundreds of employees.

GLOBAL:

- A new computing architecture emerges.
- A major technology corporation changes strategy.
- An international cyber incident occurs.
- A global supply shortage affects hardware.
- A new internet standard becomes widely adopted.
- An economic recession affects technology investment.

Events must have causes, consequences, affected entities, and historical records.

14. COMPLEX EMERGENT ECONOMY

Expand the economic simulation into a complete interconnected system.

Include:

- Employment markets.
- Housing markets.
- Hardware markets.
- Software markets.
- Hosting markets.
- Cloud computing markets.
- Advertising markets.
- Subscription services.
- Freelance marketplaces.
- Intellectual property.
- Business acquisitions.
- Venture capital.
- Loans.
- Insurance.
- Taxes.
- International trade.

Prices must respond to supply, demand, competition, production costs, innovation, and economic conditions.

Introduce inflation, interest rates, unemployment, recessions, growth cycles, and financial crises.

All financial activity must remain simulated and use fictional in-game assets.

15. PERSONAL PROJECT ECOSYSTEM

Allow players to maintain multiple projects simultaneously.

Examples:

- A personal website.
- A software application.
- A game studio.
- A hosting business.
- A social network.
- An AI service.
- A research project.
- A marketplace.
- A private server network.
- An online publication.

Projects have development stages, resources, expenses, dependencies, users, maintenance requirements, and potential revenue.

NPCs can discover, use, review, contribute to, compete with, or purchase player projects.

16. WORLD HISTORY AND LEGACY

Create a permanent historical record of civilization.

Record:

- Founding of companies.
- Technological discoveries.
- Network expansions.
- Major software releases.
- Business failures.
- Economic crises.
- Important NPC lives.
- Community movements.
- Major infrastructure projects.
- Political decisions.
- Player achievements.

Allow players to explore historical timelines and understand how the world evolved.

A company founded by an NPC years ago should have a history that can be investigated.

The world should develop recognizable historical eras.

17. DEEP SIMULATION ARCHITECTURE

Implement a unified simulation framework.

All systems must share consistent data and influence one another.

Examples:

- A new GPU architecture reduces AI hosting costs.
- Lower hosting costs allow new AI startups to emerge.
- New startups recruit developers.
- Increased hiring changes salaries.
- New services attract users.
- Increased traffic creates network demand.
- Network demand encourages infrastructure investment.
- Infrastructure investment creates new jobs.

This interconnected causality is essential.

Use:

- Hierarchical simulation.
- Event-driven architecture.
- Deterministic simulation where appropriate.
- Persistent entity identifiers.
- Efficient NPC abstraction.
- Regional simulation.
- Background progression.
- Historical event logs.
- Incremental saving.
- Recoverable world states.

Avoid expensive continuous simulation of irrelevant entities.

18. USER INTERFACE EXPANSION

Preserve the realistic Linux workstation aesthetic.

The main interface should remain centered around the terminal.

Add optional integrated applications:

- File manager.
- Web browser.
- Network monitor.
- System monitor.
- Code editor.
- Email client.
- Messaging client.
- Market terminal.
- Company management.
- Cloud dashboard.
- Server administration.
- Social platform.
- World map.
- Research database.

Applications should represent actual simulation systems, not decorative menus.

Maintain an intuitive mobile interface suitable for Android screens.

19. DEVELOPMENT RULES

This is an expansion of the existing game, not a replacement.

Strictly preserve:

- Existing working terminal commands.
- Existing save data compatibility.
- Existing player identity.
- Existing economic systems.
- Existing NPCs.
- Existing companies.
- Existing market history.
- Existing world state.

Use versioned save migrations when new systems require additional data.

All new systems must integrate with existing entity IDs and shared simulation state.

Avoid creating disconnected features that do not interact with the world.

Prioritize functional mechanics over decorative interfaces.

Do not claim a system is implemented until it is actually playable and tested.

FINAL VISION

Create a complete digital civilization simulator where technology, economics, human society, business, science, politics, culture, infrastructure, and personal life evolve together.

The player should be able to spend hundreds of hours building a life inside this world without exhausting its possibilities.

They might become a programmer, researcher, entrepreneur, corporate executive, network engineer, investor, creator, or simply an ordinary internet user.

The world must not exist to serve the player.

The player exists inside the world.

INTERNET: PERSISTENT WORLD — A LIVING DIGITAL CIVILIZATION, NOT JUST A GAME ABOUT COMPUTERS."

## Objective
- Complete and validate the expansion of “INTERNET: PERSISTENT WORLD” into a persistent, autonomous digital civilization while preserving all existing gameplay systems.

## Requirements
- Expand geopolitics, geography, society, education, business, hardware, science, media, culture, law, personal life, careers, infrastructure, events, economy, projects, history, multiplayer, and UI.
- Preserve terminal commands, saves, player identity, economy, NPCs, companies, market history, world state, and existing systems.
- Add world evolution during absence, bounded and deterministic NPC simulation, persistent IDs, migration, recoverable saves, and large/offline progression validation.
- Keep new mechanics interconnected and playable rather than decorative.
- Maintain a Linux workstation aesthetic and usable mobile interface.

## Decisions
- Use `tickWorld()` as the primary civilization integration point.
- Restore missing growth metadata only in `reviveGame()`.
- Keep `30` companies, `420` NPCs, `180` servers, `220` sites, and `60` open contracts.
- Initialize `lastRentDay` from world time only when missing.
- Advance offline simulation in bounded chunks.
- Keep news and feed caps at `70` and `80` entries.

## Work State
### Completed
- Integrated bounded growth for companies, NPCs, servers, sites, contracts, news, and events into `tickWorld()`.
- Added growth metadata and compatibility restoration for older saves, including `lastRentDay`.
- Added civilization systems, interfaces, ledger, history, and multiplayer state in `src/civilization.js`.
- Wired civilization into `src/world.js`, `src/main.js`, and `src/shell.js`.
- Added civilization shell commands under `civ`.
- Fixed the initial `TLDs` typo and added the `TLDS` form.
- Passed prior syntax checks, save/revival serialization, a 5,000-world-minute smoke test, and `git diff --check`.
- The 5,000-minute smoke test reached 21 companies, 119 NPCs, 198 servers, 88 sites, and 20 contracts.

### Active
- Retrieve and address prioritized findings from the completed civilization code review.
- Run broader civilization progression, save/reload, and offline-simulation validation.
- Inspect the final diff and complete final syntax and whitespace checks.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Incorporate prioritized code-review findings for `src/civilization.js` and its integrations.
2. Run `/tmp/opencode/civ-check.mjs` and address any failing validation setup or implementation.
3. Add or verify broader coverage for 3-year progression and large offline workloads.
4. Inspect the final diff and rerun syntax and `git diff --check` validation.

## Relevant Files
- `src/civilization.js`: Civilization systems, player interfaces, ledger, history, and multiplayer state.
- `src/world.js`: Primary world tick, growth metadata, save revival, and civilization integration.
- `src/main.js`: Persistence, offline progression/reporting, and civilization imports.
- `src/shell.js`: Terminal commands and civilization gameplay interfaces.
- `src/systems.js`: Auxiliary cloud, container, agent, and organization systems.

messages.text:
"INTERNET: PERSISTENT WORLD

ULTIMATE EXPANSION III — DIGITAL CIVILIZATION

Integrate the following systems into the existing game without removing or simplifying previously implemented features.

The objective is to create a comprehensive simulation of modern human civilization connected through a persistent digital ecosystem.

All systems must interact with the same world, economy, NPC population, databases, and historical timeline.

A. GLOBAL COUNTRIES AND GEOPOLITICS

Create a simulated world containing multiple countries and regions.

Each country has:

- Government.
- Political institutions.
- Economy.
- Currency.
- Population.
- Internet infrastructure.
- Telecommunications providers.
- Taxation system.
- Digital regulations.
- Financial institutions.
- Universities.
- Technology industries.

Simulate international relations, trade agreements, regulatory changes, technological competition, sanctions, diplomatic negotiations, and cyber policies.

Government decisions should affect businesses, individuals, investments, technology adoption, and internet accessibility.

B. LAW AND DIGITAL GOVERNANCE

Create an evolving legal system.

Include:

- Digital privacy laws.
- Intellectual property.
- Copyright.
- Software licensing.
- Business registration.
- Employment regulations.
- Financial regulations.
- Consumer protection.
- Cybercrime legislation.
- Data protection.
- Cryptocurrency regulations.
- Digital contracts.

NPC organizations and players must be subject to applicable simulated regulations.

Introduce courts, regulatory authorities, compliance departments, lawyers, investigators, and legal disputes.

Consequences must depend on the jurisdiction and circumstances.

C. COMPLETE EDUCATION SYSTEM

Create schools, colleges, universities, online learning platforms, and independent training institutions.

NPCs can:

- Study programming.
- Learn cybersecurity.
- Study finance.
- Learn mathematics.
- Research artificial intelligence.
- Obtain certifications.
- Attend university.
- Publish research.
- Become teachers.
- Develop professional expertise.

Players can independently study subjects through realistic documentation, tutorials, laboratories, programming challenges, and educational resources.

Knowledge should be transferable to practical gameplay.

D. SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH AND DISCOVERY

Create an autonomous research ecosystem.

Universities, corporations, independent researchers, and laboratories can pursue discoveries.

Research fields include:

- Computer science.
- Artificial intelligence.
- Robotics.
- Semiconductor engineering.
- Cryptography.
- Quantum computing.
- Telecommunications.
- Materials science.
- Energy technology.
- Biotechnology.

Discoveries must require research time, funding, equipment, expertise, and experimentation.

New technologies should influence the world economy and create new industries.

Do not randomly invent impossible technologies. Maintain plausible technological dependencies and development timelines.

E. MEDIA AND INFORMATION ECOSYSTEM

Create autonomous media organizations.

Include:

- Newspapers.
- Online magazines.
- Television networks.
- Independent journalists.
- Social media platforms.
- Streaming services.
- Video creators.
- Podcasts.
- Advertising agencies.
- Public relations companies.

NPCs can create content, build audiences, publish news, produce entertainment, and monetize their work.

Information spreads through social networks according to audience size, trust, relevance, and sharing behavior.

Simulate misinformation, corrections, investigative journalism, media competition, and public opinion.

F. PHYSICAL WORLD AND INFRASTRUCTURE

Expand the simulated world beyond the internet.

Create interconnected cities with:

- Residential areas.
- Commercial districts.
- Offices.
- Industrial zones.
- Universities.
- Hospitals.
- Data centers.
- Warehouses.
- Shops.
- Transportation networks.

Simulate electricity, telecommunications, water, transportation, logistics, and physical equipment.

Infrastructure failures should affect digital services.

A regional electricity outage could interrupt data centers.

A damaged fiber-optic connection could increase latency.

A shortage of semiconductor components could delay hardware production.

G. REAL ESTATE AND PROPERTY ECONOMY

Allow NPCs and players to acquire:

- Apartments.
- Houses.
- Offices.
- Commercial buildings.
- Industrial facilities.
- Data centers.
- Warehouses.
- Land.

Simulate rent, maintenance, mortgages, property taxes, construction, insurance, and real estate market fluctuations.

Businesses can purchase offices, expand facilities, and establish regional headquarters.

NPCs can move between properties based on employment, income, family circumstances, and preferences.

H. GLOBAL SUPPLY CHAINS

Create a complex production and distribution economy.

Businesses depend on suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, transportation providers, and customers.

Track:

- Raw materials.
- Components.
- Semiconductor availability.
- Hardware manufacturing.
- Inventory.
- Shipping.
- Warehousing.
- Energy costs.
- Production capacity.

Products must require actual resources and manufacturing processes within the simulation.

Supply shortages, transportation disruptions, and rising production costs should influence market prices and company profitability.

I. AUTONOMOUS TECHNOLOGY INDUSTRY

Create competing technology ecosystems.

Companies can independently develop:

- Operating systems.
- Programming languages.
- Development tools.
- AI models.
- CPUs and GPUs.
- Networking equipment.
- Smartphones.
- Cloud platforms.
- Databases.
- Security software.
- Developer frameworks.

Technologies should have versions, compatibility, licensing, documentation, and adoption rates.

Companies can compete for market share.

Open-source projects can become major industry standards.

J. ENTERTAINMENT AND DIGITAL CULTURE

Create an independent entertainment ecosystem.

Include:

- Gaming studios.
- Online games.
- Music platforms.
- Streaming services.
- Digital art.
- Content creators.
- Virtual communities.
- Esports organizations.
- Digital events.

NPCs can create games, publish music, form communities, participate in tournaments, and develop creative careers.

Players can build entertainment companies and publish their own products.

K. DIGITAL IDENTITY AND REPUTATION

Create a unified identity system.

Each individual has:

- Personal accounts.
- Professional profiles.
- Public reputation.
- Private relationships.
- Digital credentials.
- Employment history.
- Published work.
- Financial identity.
- Security history.

Reputation must be contextual.

A person can be respected professionally but controversial in a social community.

A developer can become famous within a programming ecosystem without being famous to the general population.

L. DYNAMIC WORLD EVENTS

Introduce long-term emergent events.

Examples:

- A major technological revolution.
- A global financial recession.
- A telecommunications disruption.
- A new software standard.
- A corporate monopoly investigation.
- A major scientific discovery.
- A regional energy crisis.
- A new internet infrastructure project.
- A major cybersecurity incident.
- A global supply shortage.

Events should emerge from interconnected simulation systems.

They must create consequences that can persist for years of simulated time.

M. MULTIPLAYER AND SHARED CIVILIZATION

Design the architecture to support optional multiplayer.

Allow multiple human players to inhabit the same persistent world.

Players can:

- Start companies together.
- Employ each other.
- Trade assets.
- Develop software.
- Establish communities.
- Own infrastructure.
- Compete in markets.
- Build organizations.
- Negotiate contracts.

The world must remain functional if other players disconnect.

NPCs should continue filling the economic and social ecosystem.

Implement authoritative server-side financial transactions, permission controls, secure identity management, anti-cheat systems, and persistent shared world states.

N. LIVING HISTORICAL TIMELINE

Maintain a complete world history.

Record:

- New businesses.
- Scientific discoveries.
- Political decisions.
- Market crashes.
- Technological releases.
- Major NPC achievements.
- Wars and diplomatic events within the fictional world.
- Infrastructure development.
- Social movements.
- Cultural changes.

Allow players to explore historical timelines, discover past events, and investigate how the world reached its current state.

O. WORLD SIMULATION INTELLIGENCE

Create an interconnected simulation architecture with several levels.

1. Individual simulation: needs, personality, memory and decisions.
2. Household simulation: relationships, housing and shared finances.
3. Organization simulation: employees, management and business objectives.
4. City simulation: infrastructure, population and economic activity.
5. Country simulation: institutions, regulations and economic conditions.
6. Global simulation: trade, technology, finance and geopolitical relationships.
7. Internet simulation: networks, services, data and communication.

Changes at one level must propagate to relevant other levels.

Use efficient event-driven processing and abstraction.

- A business owner.

- A journalist.
- A digital entrepreneur.
- A software developer.
- An independent citizen.
